item.title: Pope Leo, Weeks After Surgery, Holds Up Well on South America Trip
item.description:
Flying with Pope Leo XIV over the Andes, halfway through the pontiff’s 12-day trip to South America, the journalists traveling at the back of the plane suspected something was amiss.

They had expected the pope to come out from behind the business-class curtain and take questions, as he had on previous papal flights. Instead, Vatican officials abruptly told the press corps that the pope would not be speaking with them on the nearly five-hour flight from Argentina to Peru.

Was the pope, who had been diagnosed with lung cancer less than a month earlier, feeling ill? Was he too exhausted to talk? Was he taking a nap?

“It’s evident he’s well,” said Maria Montserrat Alvarado, who heads the Vatican’s communications department, when asked why the pope wasn’t taking questions. “He’s running circles around us.”

It was perhaps inevitable that Leo’s every action on this journey, so soon after surgery to remove a lobe of his right lung, would be scrutinized for signs of fatigue or illness, particularly as the Vatican is not known for its transparency.

The three-country trip, which began in Uruguay and concludes in Peru on Monday, involves a grueling schedule of 12 flights, two helicopter rides, nine Masses, 36 speeches and numerous meetings with local bishops and community members.

Despite the journalists’ midair concerns, the pope showed no visible difficulty as he descended the staircase in Lima onto a red carpet to greet Peru’s president, Keiko Fujimori, and accept flowers from two children. Videos soon emerged showing what Leo did during the flight instead of taking questions from reporters: He visited the cockpit and talked to the air traffic control tower.

Throughout the trip, Leo has appeared robust and confident. He has walked up and down stairs, rode around — often standing — in his popemobile, blessed babies (including some dressed to look like him), leaned down to hug people in wheelchairs, sang along with hymns and local anthems, and spoken in a strong voice during his homilies and speeches.

At a vigil for youth at a stadium in Lima, he caught a rosary a young woman threw at him as he passed in the popemobile, and then effortlessly tossed it back. He has seemed equally adroit mentally. At one point in Peru, his home for years, he accidentally started a speech in Italian, then quickly switched to Spanish, laughing and apologizing. “Here, at home, and I’m speaking Italian!” he said.

The pope has visited presidential palaces and impoverished neighborhoods, met with students and visited a prison, as well as facilities for older citizens and the disabled.

Over the weekend, he traveled by helicopter to a remote town in the Andes to celebrate Mass. On Sunday alone, he flew from Chiclayo to Cusco, a Peruvian city more than 11,000 feet above sea level. There he gave a prayer and blessing before flying again to Pucallpa, a city in the rainforest, roughly 500 feet above sea level where he watched dances by Amazonian performers.

By the time Leo led Mass in a sports field there, he looked a little sapped — but then so did those of us in the traveling press corps.

When he spoke in Cusco, his voice was clear, and he showed no hint of altitude sickness as rain pounded down around the covered platform where he stood. In the city’s central square, Plaza de Armas, the pope dedicated a prayer to those who “are suffering in body and soul because of illness.” He did not mention his own recent brush with disease.

Before the pope arrived in the square, Vanessa Loagca, 39, said she understood that “this trip is a big sacrifice for the pope’s health.” Along with her husband and two children, Ms. Loagca had slept overnight in the square to secure a spot at the front for a good view of the pope. “We feel a lot of love for him,” she said.

Lung specialists said the pope’s stamina fell within a normal range but was still notable.

“Most patients that I know wouldn’t be so active this soon after surgery,” said Dr. Natalie Liu, a thoracic surgeon and oncologist at Stanford University Hospital. “But I also feel like he probably has a lot of incentive and purpose in his life.”

The trip to Peru, in particular, has been significant for Leo, who served there for 20 years as a missionary, priest and bishop and became a Peruvian citizen. He is “going back home, honoring his country, feeling the love from his people,” said Prof. Christopher D. Tirres, an expert on Latin America at Santa Clara University.

On occasion, Leo has noted the concerns about his health. On the flight from Rome to Montevideo, Uruguay, the first stop on the trip, the pope told reporters that he knew some people wondered if he would be able to travel so soon after surgery. “From the first day I had no doubt, and was convinced that this trip had to go forward,” he said.

And in Lima, speaking to a group of bishops, priests and nuns at a prayer service at a cathedral, he took a gibe at the “doubting Thomases” who had predicted that he would postpone the journey. “But God is great and his grace is bigger than all of us, and I’m very happy to be here with you,” he said.

Some of the faithful said they feared the pope might be overextending himself.

“His condition was delicate,” said Donaldo Rodríguez, 60, at the Mass outside Chiclayo. “He’s come out because he has a commitment to the Lord to serve the people, but I don’t think he should have come. He needs to take care of himself. He really ought to be resting after all this.”

With modern surgical techniques, most patients “are back to their base line” within two to four weeks after the procedure, said Dr. Zaid Abdelsattar, a thoracic surgeon at Loyola Medicine in Chicago. Dr. Abdelsattar said that while some fatigue could be expected, patients “can live their life to the fullest, just like they have been before.” That is particularly the case if they were otherwise healthy before the surgery and the cancer was caught early, as was the case with Leo, he said.

Even if the pope appears to have recovered from his health scare, he will face regular screenings for the next five years. “There is still a chance that the lung cancer can come back,” said Dr. Abdelsattar.

For many, Leo’s presence was an inspiration.

Francisco de la Cruz Barrera, 67, whose leg was amputated after a motorcycle accident, was pushed in a wheelchair to attend the pope’s Mass near Chiclayo. Mr. de la Cruz said it was important for him to be there because he believed God had given him another chance after his crash.

Leo, Mr. de la Cruz said, “seems quite strong.” But given the pope’s recent illness, he said, “We must continue to pray for him.”

Mitra Taj contributed reporting from Chiclayo, Peru.

item.title: War May Answer Longtime Riddle of Iranian Dams Built for No Clear Reason
item.description:
Environmentalists have long been mystified by the significant proliferation of dams and water transfer projects like pipelines and tunnels across Iran, especially in regions that had no apparent need for them.

Some analysts think they now know the answer after U.S. and Israeli airstrikes on concealed Iranian missile sites this year targeted many of the same areas. These analysts have concluded that the water projects may have been developed to support the country’s military buildup.

Given the secrecy surrounding Iran’s missile program, any connection between it and Iran’s ambitious, decades-old initiative to develop water infrastructure remains speculative. But some experts find the evidence highly suggestive.

Nima Shokri, an expert on water security, and his team at the Hamburg University of Technology, in Germany, had for years tracked an unusually high number of dams across Iran — at least 533 of them, among the most of any country in the region.

“It was always puzzling to me,” he said. “Why were they building so many dams?”

In the spring, Dr. Shokri was perusing news about the war in his home country when he came across a map plotting airstrikes that had targeted suspected military sites. The pattern — a semicircle of dots from north to south — nearly matched that of his own map marking the locations of dams.

His old question, he said, was superseded by a new one: “Why does it seem that wherever we have dams, there is a missile strike close by?”

Placing sophisticated and sprawling military sites near the continuous water and power supply provided by dams would be logical, said seven water and military experts interviewed by The New York Times.

This gives Tehran “operational continuity,” said Danny Citrinowicz, a former longtime Iran analyst for Israel’s military intelligence agency.

“Iran has a strong incentive to ensure that its missile complexes are not dependent on the broader national infrastructure for essential services,” Mr. Citrinowicz said. He added that it was reasonable to assess “that Iran has invested in some degree of autonomous or redundant infrastructure,” like dams and water projects, for its missile facilities.

Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Ministry of Energy, which is partly responsible for dam construction, did not respond to requests for comment. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps, which also plays a role in dam construction, did not respond to a request either.

Iran calls the subterranean sites its “missile cities” — heavily fortified tunnels and rooms dug deep beneath the mountains, used not only to store and deploy long-range ballistic missiles and drones, but also to produce them.

Farzin Nadimi, a senior fellow with the Washington Institute and an expert on Iranian military affairs, estimates that there are at least 30 missile sites across the country. Very few countries maintain as elaborate a system of underground military sites as Iran, he said, citing North Korea as an exception.

As a country that often experiences water shortages, Iran still does need dams. “Many dams in Iran serve essential civilian purposes, including water supply, irrigation and hydropower generation, particularly in a water-scarce country. Any potential military role should not overshadow these functions,” Dr. Shokri said.

By highlighting the extent and location of concealed missile sites in remote parts of the country, the U.S. and Israeli airstrikes may also have shed light on another puzzle that has troubled environmentalists: What are the reasons behind a string of arrests in 2018 of wildlife conservationists working in protected areas?

The Revolutionary Guards, whose intelligence arm carried out the arrests, did not comment about them for this article, and a definitive explanation remains elusive. But some environmentalists said they now suspect that the conservation workers may have accidentally happened upon sensitive military sites.

In 2018, the intelligence wing of the Revolutionary Guards detained dozens of conservationists on charges of espionage. One of them, Kavous Seyed-Emami, a founder of the Persian Wildlife Heritage Foundation, died in state custody. Several other members of the group, who spent years in prison, said they were tortured and sexually harassed.

At the time, senior Iranian officials said they were unaware of the allegations of mistreatment and that they would be examined.

Iranian authorities accused the conservationists of using cameras — intended for monitoring the habitats of rare and endangered species like the Asiatic cheetah — to instead gather intelligence for the United States and Israel.

“One of the accusations leveled against me was that I had trained lizards to spy on military installations,” said Morad Tahbaz, a founder of the Persian Wildlife Heritage Foundation, who spent more than five years in prison.

Political analysts suspected an effort by the Revolutionary Guards to undermine the reformist government in power at the time, which was trying to open the country to investment and expertise in various sectors including the environment.

“I think it is possible that the Guards saw anyone doing fieldwork near these sites, even wildlife conservationists, as a potential security threat,” said Nik Kowsar, a prominent Iranian environmental and water analyst in exile in Washington.

Kaveh Madani, who was deputy head of Iran’s department of environment when he was arrested in the 2018 crackdown, said that conservation groups never worked in wilderness areas without permission from the government and intelligence services.

The targeting of two Iranian regions in recent airstrikes provides intriguing examples.

Amir Aghakouchak, a prominent water expert at the University of California, Irvine, had long been perplexed by the construction of a massive project to transfer water from the mountainous Zagros region to central Yazd.

Airstrikes in March on the Yazd region prompted reports, including in The Financial Times, of a major missile facility in the area. Mr. Aghakouchak said he began to suspect that the water project “may have been influenced, at least in part, by military considerations.”

Mr. Tahbaz, of the wildlife heritage foundation, said he was always mystified, during his time in prison, by his interrogators’ fixation on his team’s work in Hormozgan Province, where there was a project to support the rare Laristan wild sheep. “They were incredibly sensitive about that area,” he recalled.

On July 14, U.S. airstrikes hit the Tarom Protected Area in Hormozgan, killing the family of a local wildlife ranger in the process. The U.S. military said it was targeting military infrastructure and coastal defenses. Mr. Nadimi, the military expert, said the location was not far from where military analysts believe Iran constructed a missile base deep below ground.

Environmentalists knew the area for something entirely different.

“It had a storage shed with hay,” Mr. Kowsar said, “for Laristan wild sheep.”

item.title: The Death of ‘Keep 1.5 Alive’
item.description:
There was a reason, 11 years ago in Paris, that world leaders set themselves a target to keep the global rise in temperatures below 1.5 degrees Celsius compared with preindustrial levels. Beyond that, climate scientists say, warming will dangerously change our way of life.

We got a taste of it this year, as temperatures rose above the threshold for several months. Heat waves. Wildfires. Flash floods. And with a super El Niño year unfolding, next year might be worse. As one climate expert put it to me: This El Niño will effectively offer a time machine to the 2030s, showing what will happen if we don’t radically cut carbon emissions.

My colleague David Gelles, host of the Climate Forward newsletter, has been following the much diminished U.N. climate talks in Turkey. Today he writes about the death of 1.5 degrees and what that means for the planet.

By David Gelles

It was the climate movement’s unifying slogan for the past decade: “Keep 1.5 Alive.”

The tagline referred to the central ambition of the 2015 Paris climate agreement, in which almost every country pledged to try to limit global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius.

Now, just 11 years after the target was set, it’s effectively dead.

Scientists now say that without increasingly drastic efforts to reduce greenhouse gases — more drastic than the ones humans have tried and failed at so far — it is very likely that the planet will warm at least 2.6ºC by the end of the century.

At COP31, the ongoing United Nations climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, diplomats who spent so long championing the 1.5 degree target have been blunt.

“The world has no chance of holding to 1.5 degrees,” said Chris Bowen, Australia’s minister for climate change and energy, who is leading the negotiations.

Tipping points

Scientists for years have warned that allowing global average temperatures to rise 1.5ºC, compared with preindustrial levels, would result in a profoundly more dangerous world. Extreme heat will become more common and intense. Storms will become more powerful and destructive. Sea levels will rise. And poor countries will bear the brunt of the damage.

That scenario is already playing out around the world. In recent months, wildfires have raged from Canada to Indonesia. The collapse of a glacier in Nepal killed thousands and wiped away towns. Floods and mudslides devastated Brazil. And a summer of European heat waves killed an estimated 50,000 people.

Should warming continue unabated, scientists say the world may cross certain tipping points, including the melting of Arctic permafrost, the rapid decline of rainforests and a slowdown of a key current in the Atlantic Ocean.

The 1.5 degrees target was always ambitious. Achieving it would have required wealthy countries to make the biggest changes, with potentially profound effects on their economies. Cost, politics and inertia all got in the way.

As a result, one big question at the climate talks has been whether the world should set a new goal. But most people I spoke with said no.

“We don’t think that there’s a new target,” said Ilana Seid, Palau’s ambassador to the United Nations. “We still have a Paris Agreement target of 1.5, and so we are still continuing to say that’s the target.”

Rachel Cleetus, director of the climate program at the Union of Concerned Scientists, warned against picking a new target, saying that it was important to confront what breaching the threshold has wrought.

“I don’t think it’s a question of replacing 1.5,” she said. “There is no new number. We are now in the unsafe zone.”

Leaders rejected the idea of resetting the goal to 2ºC or even 2.5ºC, saying that allowing for endless revisions created a slippery slope that could make progress harder to achieve.

A temporary breach?

While world leaders acknowledged they had missed the target, they also said it might still be possible to get back to 1.5 degrees of warming.

The United Nations secretary general, António Guterres, called on countries to redouble efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions with the aim of limiting additional warming, and ultimately turning down Earth’s thermostat.

“The truth is that we have the power to determine how high, how long and how devastating that overshoot will be,” he said. “We have the power to make sure the overshoot is a temporary breach, not a permanent sentence.”

So far, the world has crossed the 1.5 threshold for only a few months. But emissions continue at near-record levels. Although clean energy is growing rapidly, the world is expected to continue to use fossil fuels for decades to come.

At this point, meeting the emissions targets set in Paris wouldn’t be enough to bring the temperature rise back down from 1.5 degrees. It would require drastic reductions in the burning of fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas — and possibly more.

Because reducing emissions is proving so difficult, some environmentalists and scientists are proposing different types of geoengineering. These include large-scale carbon capture and storage or attempts to reflect the sun’s energy away from the planet by injecting particulate matter into the stratosphere.

“Overshoot must be kept as small and short as possible, and be rapidly reversed,” said Hilda Heine, president of the Marshall Islands, an island nation threatened by sea-level rise. “We have fallen short of the emissions reductions needed to stay under 1.5. We must rewrite the future.”

item.title: Debt Problems of the Richest Countries Are Trickling Down to the Poorest
item.description:
It’s hard to find a government these days that is not struggling with crushing public debt.

The financial problems of wealthier nations have been monopolizing the spotlight. The United States, Britain, France, Italy, China and Japan are all facing record or near-record debt levels. The fallout has been painfully visible in France, where anger at rising costs and crumbling public facilities and services helped provoke violent protests and a general strike in recent weeks.

But rich countries’ fiscal problems do not just pool at home; they trickle down to amplify the financial pressures on low and middle-income countries.

The result is that less-well off nations are borrowing more and paying more for their loans. Their combined debt surged last year to $9.4 trillion, according to a World Bank report this month.

The poorest of the poor countries fare the worst: They are facing interest rates not seen since the late 1980s.

Many of the causes are beyond their control. A series of crises, beginning with the Covid-19 pandemic, and continuing with energy shocks, supply chain disruptions and rising prices stemming from the wars in Ukraine and Iran have strained national budgets and pumped up debts.

Surging inflation pushed central banks to raise interest rates, which in turn has contributed to higher borrowing costs around the world.

“Debts that previously looked completely reasonable suddenly were carrying interest burdens that were well in excess of what a developing country can really afford to be paying,” said Christina Segal-Knowles, managing director, international policy at the Rockefeller Foundation. “That has led many countries to get in a really pernicious cycle.”

Big debts in wealthier nations are also affecting countries lower down the income latter. Bond yields — the returns paid to buyers of government debt — are surging around the world. Private investors, increasingly worried about ballooning deficits and other challenges, are demanding to be paid more for taking on the risk of lending even to wealthy countries when they fear political leaders are shirking hard financial choices.

The U.S. bond market — the world’s largest and most consequential — helps drive what happens elsewhere. U.S. Treasuries are widely considered the safest in the world. But a federal debt of more than $40 trillion, roughly 120 percent of the size of the American economy, has aroused concerns.

Mounting deficits and the administration’s policies have helped push yields on U.S. Treasuries past 5 percent, reaching levels not seen in two decades. In France, bond yields are at a 25-year high, while Japanese bond yields are trading at their highest levels in three decades.

In turn, lower and middle-income countries, whose economies are nowhere near as strong as the United States, must offer even heftier premiums to compete.

The Ivory Coast, Kenya and Nigeria, for example, have had to promise lenders annual interest rates ranging from 7.5 to more than 10 percent.

Paying so much money to borrow is often necessary in the short term but self-defeating in the long run. Growth levels in these countries are unlikely to generate enough income to be able to pay off these loans.

Borrowing from institutions like the International Monetary Fund has also become more expensive for all but the poorest countries. That’s because the rates offered by the fund are based on interest rates set by key central banks.

“You see how the actions of the central banks of the advanced economies determine the cost of borrowing,” said Martin Guzman, a professor at Columbia University and a former economics minister of Argentina. “Ecuador has nothing to do with the war in Ukraine or Iran, but somehow they end up paying a higher interest rate to the I.M.F.”

And the Federal Reserve and other major central banks are expected to remain under pressure to raise rates further.

The high cost of repaying existing loans and accessing new ones are constricting political leaders’ ability to govern, regardless of their ideological bent. With so much money being redirected to pay down debts, there is less and less available to pay for education, health care, pensions, infrastructure, economic development and more.

In Egypt, Pakistan and Tunisia, more money is flowing out of the countries to cover debt and interest payments than they are receiving in loans, Mr. Guzman said.

Fifty-one countries, home to 3.7 billion people, spend more on interest payments than on health care or education, according to the United Nations Trade and Development.

At the same time, foreign aid and low-interest loans from advanced economies and multilateral development banks have dried up. China, which went on a lending binge in the 2010s, is now more focused on collecting money than on handing it out.

Mavis Owusu-Gyamfi, president and chief executive of the African Center for Economic Transformation, underscored the need for joint action.

“China is a big player in this game and until we can reach a consensus with them,” she said, “every single debt negotiation is going to be in bits and pieces and is going to take a long time.”

What’s particularly frustrating is that money designated to promote growth is being siphoned off. Countries that receive lower-interest loans from international financial institutions like the World Bank or regional development banks end up using some of that money to repay private lenders instead of investing in businesses or creating jobs.

Many emerging economies in deep debt have avoided default, but not necessarily because they have achieved financial stability. Instead, they have prioritized repaying their loans.

“It means defaulting on development rather than on debts,” Mr. Guzman said.

Creditors demand higher returns for riskier loans, he points out, but when the risk materializes, they balk at accepting less than they are owed.

The Rockefeller Foundation and other organizations are pushing for lenders to agree to break the cycle — to temporarily postpone repayments that drain governmental resources and kill off prospects for longer-term growth.

At a time when aid and other assistance is tight, Ms. Segal-Knowles at Rockefeller argues, international financial institutions can also do more to use existing resources — like gold reserves — as financial leverage to free up money for affordable development loans.

She pointed to a $21 million loan from the United States to the I.M.F.’s poverty reduction and growth trust in 2024. The money enabled the fund to generate an astounding $21 billion in loans to developing nations.

“This is just one great example of how inexpensive it can be to mobilize I.M.F. and World Bank resources,” she said.

item.title: A Beloved Penguin Mascot Is Retiring in Japan. Some Fans Are Bereft.
item.description:
For more than two decades, train commuters in Japan have had a faithful companion on their daily journeys: the Suica penguin. But the little black-and-white bird will soon take its last ride.

One of Japan’s largest rail operators adopted the penguin as the mascot for its prepaid smart cards, known as Suica cards, in 2001. On the cards, the penguin is smiling and waving as it walks.

The East Japan Railway Company, or JR East, announced the character’s retirement last year, and in September the company held an international public vote to pick a new mascot.

On Wednesday, the company will announce which new character will replace the penguin. And in a country that loves its mascots, many people have strong opinions.

On Monday afternoon, at Sakuragicho railway station, southwest of Tokyo, customers at a store selling merchandise featuring the Suica penguin lamented the loss of a familiar presence.

“I was really shocked when it was announced that the character would be ‘graduating,’” said Eriko Inoue, using JR East’s term for the outgoing penguin. Ms. Inoue, 50, a part-time nursery teacher, was stocking up on merchandise in case the company discontinued some of it after the penguin’s retirement.

“He’s just become a natural, constant presence in my life — he’s on my commuter card, he’s on station billboards,” Ms. Inoue said. She had picked up a clear folder file and a Suica card case featuring the penguin.

The penguin will be retired in March, and its replacement will take over in April.

The three contenders for JR East’s new mascot are a brown squirrel with rosy cheeks; a bright purple rabbit with a wide grin and a blank, thousand-yard stare; and an orange creature wearing only an anxious expression, a pair of boots and a bag with a mole in it. (Japanese news media outlets say that it belongs to “no particular species.”)

Ms. Inoue said she had long been a fan of Chiharu Sakazaki, the illustrator who created the penguin. She added that she was aware of the vote for a new mascot, but had chosen not to participate.

“I’m too attached to the penguin,” she said.

Noriko Tanaka, 60, who was also at the store picking up some penguin merchandise, said she had voted for the bunny character, which she described as having a “creepy-cute vibe.” The other two felt somewhat generic, she said.

Online, the purple rabbit has become a source of memes, embraced by people who say its blank eyes and garish smile are indicative of a heart of darkness.

People have made A.I.-generated videos of the rabbit chasing people down, lurking on abandoned railway platforms and beating up the other two characters. (In other, more heartwarming videos, the rabbit is ultimately revealed to be warm and affectionate despite its ominous appearance.)

Ms. Tanaka said that she was fond of the penguin, even as someone who didn’t generally like mascots.

“It’s monochromatic and doesn’t have an overly aggressive or sharp look,” she said. “It’s something that appeals to everyone, from little kids to adults, to even someone like me, who’s practically a grandmother now. It just feels very approachable, doesn’t it?”

Even some who had no particular affection for the Suica penguin said they felt slightly bereft upon learning of its retirement.

Yuta Sekijo only found out about the penguin’s impending retirement when asked about it by a New York Times reporter. He said he went to the store to pick up some merchandise for his wife, adding that he was indifferent to the character, and to mascots in general. Still, he said, “I think I’ll feel a bit sad about it.”

Ms. Tanaka wondered whether the authorities would keep the penguin character in some form, even if it was no longer the official mascot.

“Even if the design on the Suica card itself changes, it would be nice if the character could still stick around,” she said.

item.title: Trump Has Praised Marcos’s Family Legacy. His Father Was a Dictator.
item.description:
President Trump’s stopover at the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit is part of a state visit to the Philippines, where he will be received with a 21-gun salute.

The last time he met President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. of the Philippines, was full of praise for the Filipino leader.

“Great family, great family legacy and highly respected in his country,” Mr. Trump said while hosting Mr. Marcos at the White House last year.

But that legacy was long considered an obstacle to Mr. Marcos’s political ambitions. He is the son of the dictator Ferdinand E. Marcos, who ruled the Philippines for 20 years, imposed martial law and was ousted in 1986 by a nonviolent uprising. The elder Marcos died in exile in Hawaii, without facing trial on U.S. criminal charges that he had plundered the Philippine Treasury. Years later, a court found his estate liable for torture, summary executions and disappearances.

The younger Marcos spent years rehabilitating his family’s image and won election in 2022. He is hosting Mr. Trump at his official residence, Malacañang Palace, which was also his childhood home.

Mr. Marcos and his wife, Liza Marcos, will receive Mr. Trump on Wednesday with a 21-gun salute. Mr. Trump is expected to sign the palace guest book, hold closed-door meetings, pose for a handshake, then attend a state luncheon held in his honor.

It is not clear whether Mr. Trump, who has a well-known affinity for autocratic leaders, will meet with Mr. Marcos’s mother, Imelda, 97, with whom he has socialized in New York. Ms. Marcos wielded immense power when her husband was president and later came to be known for her flamboyant lifestyle, shoe collection and unexplained wealth.

Mr. Marcos has said that when he called to congratulate Mr. Trump on his election victory in November 2024, Mr. Trump asked about Imelda Marcos.

“My mother is really his friend, he knows my mother very well,” Mr. Marcos said, relaying the conversation. “He was asking about her, ‘How’s Imelda?’ I told him she sends her congratulations.”

After the pomp and circumstance at Malacañang, which traces its roots to the Spanish colonial era in the Philippines, Mr. Trump is headed to Shenzhen, China. The highlight of that leg of his trip will be a trilateral meeting with two strongmen: President Xi Jinping of China and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia.

item.title: Here’s the latest.
item.description:
President Trump on Tuesday began a whirlwind Asia trip in which he will meet Xi Jinping of China and other world leaders, with an unpredictable agenda that could include the future of American tariffs, nuclear arms control and U.S. restrictions on advanced artificial intelligence chips.

Mr. Trump landed in Manila, where he is scheduled to meet with President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. of the Philippines and attend a gathering of Southeast Asian leaders. After less than 24 hours there, he will head to the APEC economic summit in Shenzhen, China, where all eyes will be on his expected meeting with Mr. Xi and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia.

The brief itinerary appears to reflect Mr. Trump’s preferences. He dislikes big summits where he often is not the sole subject of attention. And he enjoys meeting with leaders of powerful nations — especially Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin, two authoritarian leaders he often talks about in admiring terms.

Mr. Trump will be meeting Mr. Xi for the third time this year, and a three-way meeting between China, Russia and the United States would be the first of its kind. Each leader will arrive at the session, planned for Thursday, with a different agenda, and some analysts have compared it to Yalta, where the leaders of the United States, Britain and the Soviet Union divided up postwar Europe in 1945.

That analogy has limits: No one thinks these three leaders, powerful as they are, are there to redefine the borders of any continent. But their very presence at one table would underscore they have major sway over the shape of the next world order. And for Mr. Trump, who loves the symbolism of a dramatic photo op, that may be enough.

On Tuesday, Mr. Trump will catch the end of a dayslong meeting of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.

He isn’t just any latecomer: He is the one who issued tariffs on countries across the region, even on allies — bolstering the feeling in Asia that the United States is not a reliable partner, but rather one that treasures its commercial interests over its security interests. Southeast Asian leaders will be looking for any signs that the Republican defeat in the midterm elections may have humbled Mr. Trump or made him reconsider his policies.

Mr. Trump will also meet with leaders from the so-called “Quad” — the United States, India, Japan and Australia. All three partners are smarting from high energy prices triggered by the Iran war, a conflict Mr. Trump never discussed with them before launching it in late February.

Before leaving for China on Wednesday, Mr. Trump will be hosted by Mr. Marcos, who has been contending with Chinese challenges to islands that both Beijing and Manila claim.

In Shenzhen — the heart of China’s robotics and A.I. industries — Mr. Trump will pursue détente with Mr. Xi. He needs to extend a soon-expiring trade truce that limited tariffs on Chinese goods entering the United States in return for a Chinese commitment not to cut off rare earths and magnets.

Then comes the main event: the meeting with Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin.

“We are going to be talking about denuclearization, a tough subject because it is very hard for any of us to say we’ll get rid of our nukes,’’ Mr. Trump told reporters before leaving Washington, referring to the agenda of the trilateral meeting. “We will talk about Iran a little,” he said, insisting the situation was in “very good shape.”

Mr. Trump also said he would talk about Ukraine, on which Mr. Putin’s aides are engaging in talks with the U.S. and Ukrainian officials, but also renewing demands that NATO pull back its troops to where they were before the alliance expanded toward Russia.

On nuclear weapons, Chinese officials have made clear they are not interested in talks until their arsenal is roughly the size of the American one. And on the Iran war, analysts say it seems unlikely that the three-way meeting would make any progress — at a moment when Russia is happy to see energy prices remain high, and China is eager to see them rapidly decline.

Here’s what else we’re covering:

A counter to China: Last December, the United States launched an initiative called Pax Silica to unite partners around A.I. supply chains independent of China. In the Philippines, America’s oldest ally in Asia, the backlash has been fierce. Read more ›

Philippine leader: President Trump’s well-known affinity for autocratic leaders was on display the last time he met with President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. of the Philippines. Read more ›

item.title: As Trump Goes to China, A.I. Tensions Surge Amid Spying and Safety Fears
item.description:
When President Trump and Xi Jinping, the leader of China, met earlier this fall, they sounded committed to finding common ground on calibrating the rapid development of advanced artificial intelligence.

“We have both the capability and responsibility to develop and manage A.I. for good and ensure that the development of A.I. is always under human control and serves the well-being of the people,” Mr. Xi said in September in the grand foyer of the White House.

Mr. Trump leaned into that spirit, saying, “The decisions we make in these areas today can promote peace and prosperity for decades and decades to come.” But he has called fears of A.I. threats a “hoax,” and earlier that week said at the United Nations that he would label artificial intelligence “super intelligence” to give it a better branding.

On the eve of their third leadership summit of the year, the two men and their administrations have made little if any progress on negotiating A.I. safety issues and development guidelines, despite growing fears about the technology, current and former U.S. officials say.

And that was before Jensen Huang was forced to resign last week as chief executive of Nvidia, the U.S. technology giant that supplies computer chips fueling the A.I. boom.

Mr. Huang stepped down after The New York Times reported last month that the U.S. had gathered intelligence showing that a Chinese businesswoman in Singapore with whom he had a close relationship might have been secretly working or in contact with China’s main spy agency. Mr. Huang has publicly admitted that he had an affair.

Advancements in technology — and particularly on A.I. — have become a focal point in the superpowers’ economic and military rivalry in recent years, but never have those issues been more in the spotlight.

“The primary point of competition between us is certainly on A.I., quantum computing, biotech, cyber, all those issues,” said R. Nicholas Burns, a former career U.S. diplomat who was ambassador to China in the Biden administration.

“But obviously we’ve got a self-interest, and I think they do too,” he added, “in making sure the competition doesn’t veer off in a direction that would be destabilizing and potentially increase the probability of a conflict.”

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said last week that the governments have had conversations about A.I. safety “sort of at the technical level.” “Obviously, we’ve heard their perspective, they’ve heard ours, but that’s still a work in progress,” he said.

One reason there has been little momentum is that the two nations have differing views of the greatest risks posed by A.I., the current and former U.S. officials say.

In the United States, officials, executives and researchers talk about the possibility of A.I. becoming autonomous and working on its own outside human control or even dominating humans.

That is a concern in China, too, but its government appears to be more worried about how A.I. could be used by humans to undermine the Chinese Communist Party.

At the same time, the party’s main spy and counterintelligence agency, the Ministry of State Security, aims to use A.I. for intelligence gathering both in the country and overseas, The Times has reported.

Suspicions about espionage heighten the mutual distrust in Washington and Beijing over A.I. issues. Each side thinks the other is engaged in spying to learn more about rival A.I. secrets and to dominate development faster, the officials said.

The murky trade and spying scandal involving Mr. Huang and Nvidia looms over the meeting between Mr. Trump and Mr. Xi scheduled for Thursday in Shenzhen, a technology and manufacturing hub in southern China.

In his second term, Mr. Trump has ordered the U.S. government to loosen export restrictions to China on advanced chips. But on Monday, the Trump administration announced that it was moving forward with a new rule that would limit China’s ability to access certain chips through the use of data centers in other countries.

The policy on advanced chips is separate from the safety issues about A.I. development. The nascent dialogue on safety is being run by the Treasury Department. Critics say the talks are virtually nonexistent, though Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent insists they will happen.

The governments “expect to exchange best practices for evaluating and testing advanced models before their release, and for keeping human judgment firmly in command of this technology,” he said last week.

He added that they are “establishing a direct channel to ensure that either nation can promptly alert the other to serious incidents involving” A.I. models.

As he eventually did with Mr. Trump, Mr. Xi agreed to start a dialogue on A.I. with the Biden administration. The first meeting was held in Geneva in May 2024. Mr. Biden’s aides had hoped China would send officials from the three agencies most involved in monitoring or regulating A.I. development, including the Ministry of State Security, the spy agency.

But China sent foreign ministry officials disappointing the Americans, former U.S. officials said. The two sides made little headway.

However, that November, when Mr. Biden and Mr. Xi had their final meeting, in Lima, Peru, the two leaders announced one agreement on A.I. — that humans and not A.I. must have control over the two countries’ nuclear arsenals.

But like Mr. Trump, some Chinese officials are wary of any constraints on broader development.

For one thing, the Chinese government sees the technology as critical for addressing a coming demographic crisis. A.I. could power a wave of robot labor.

“The Chinese view any type of outreach that we are doing as a means to really keep them down or a ploy to not allow their industry to develop as rapidly as possible,” retired Gen. Paul M. Nakasone, the former head of the National Security Agency and U.S. Cyber Command, said in an onstage interview last month.

Even if China committed to an international agreement on A.I. safety, U.S. officials will likely doubt that Beijing would abide by the terms, given its history of violating past cybersecurity accords, a senior U.S. intelligence official said.

In 2015, Beijing signed an agreement with the Obama administration pledging that the two countries would not hack into each other’s companies for the purposes of stealing intellectual property. But U.S. intelligence agencies quickly concluded that China was violating the pact, the official said — and later Washington publicly accused Beijing of that.

Chinese Communist Party officials appear to think A.I., while posing new risks, could be used to monitor Chinese citizens and reinforce party control. The government’s internet regulator, the Cyberspace Administration of China, is also the A.I. overseer. That agency suppressed a relatively freewheeling Chinese internet earlier this century and transformed online space into a controlled zone that security officials use for surveillance.

On the flip side, the government’s anxiety over potential A.I. threats to party rule was made clear in a September article by Chen Yixin, the head of the main spy agency. He called for more party control over A.I. to prevent political instability, defend against cyberattacks and misinformation campaigns from “hostile forces,” and compete militarily with the United States.

Mr. Chen’s spy agency is involved in a range of activities involving A.I., including possibly gathering intelligence on Mr. Huang and other American technology executives, U.S. officials said.

The Chinese government has said the espionage concerns over Alice Huang, the Chinese executive who worked at Megaspeed, the technology company in Singapore, are a “fabrication.”

There are signs China has turned to hackers in seeking more insight into U.S. strategies on A.I.

Last month, Proofpoint, a U.S.-based cybersecurity firm, released findings accusing China-aligned hacking groups of targeting A.I. experts at American research institutes, universities and law firms. Some of them work on regulation and export issues.

The campaign relied on emails in which the hackers impersonated A.I. policymakers, including a senior one at the White House.

Proofpoint did not disclose whether the hacking attempts were successful, but it said the activity “aligns with the broader Chinese intelligence priorities amid growing U.S.-China competition over A.I., export controls and strategic technologies.”

Julian E. Barnes and Alan Rappeport contributed reporting from Washington, and Michael Crowley contributed from Paris.

item.title: There’s a New Push at Climate Talks: Wire the World for Electricity
item.description:
If the leaders of this year’s United Nations climate conference achieve one of their big goals, countries will rally behind a new global target on expanding the reach of electric power.

The implication: The rest of the world will have to look a lot more like China.

Over the past two decades, China has raced ahead of other industrialized countries, building ultrahigh-voltage power lines, constructing the world’s largest high-speed rail system and filling its roads with electric vehicles. It is sometimes called the first electrostate.

At the same time, countries across the West and in Africa are scarcely more electrified than they were a generation ago.

That disparity is one of the things the climate conference, known this year as COP31, is campaigning to change. The event’s leaders say the shift is well-suited for a year when the United States’ war in Iran has pinched the global oil and gas supply.

“Electrification is the answer,” said Murat Kurum, the Turkish environment minister, who is leading the 12-day conference in Antalya, Turkey. “Everyone now understands that energy that you must import is energy that you do not control.”

Electrification involves replacing technologies that directly burn fossil fuels. That means swapping gas-powered vehicles for E.V.s, for instance, and trading oil-fired furnaces for heat pumps. It also entails looking for electric alternatives to generate the steam and intense heat needed by factories.

Electrification doesn’t automatically imply doing away with planet-warming fossil fuels, because electrical grids — the networks of power plants, wires, transformers and substations that generate electricity and deliver it to homes and businesses — can still be powered by sources that emit greenhouse gases. But even in countries that power their grids with fossil fuels, electric machines use less energy than those that burn coal, oil and gas. Advocates for climate action tend to see electrification as a prerequisite for the transition to clean energy.

“It is the most effective approach to accelerating the transition from fossil fuels,” said Manish Bapna, the president and chief executive of the Natural Resources Defense Council.

China is currently the world’s largest polluter, and half of its grid is powered by coal. But that share is falling as it builds solar farms and wind turbines on a monumental scale. China also manufactures 70 percent of the world’s electric vehicles and 80 percent of its solar panels. There are more public E.V. charging stations in China than in all other countries combined.

China has increased its electrification rate by about 10 percentage points per decade, three times as fast as the rest of the world.

“They had the abundance agenda: build, build, build,” said Li Shuo, the director of the China Climate Hub at the Asia Society Policy Institute.

There are plenty of reasons other countries haven’t moved as quickly. The International Energy Agency notes that electrification is more cost-effective in fossil fuel-importing nations that pay high prices. China builds utility-scale projects several times as fast as the United States or Europe, according to research.

Kingsmill Bond, a strategist at Ember, a nonprofit research organization based in London that focuses on clean power, said that some European countries had been focused on adding clean energy to their grids, but not on helping their grids reach into new places.

“It’s been a massive error,” he said.

In the United States, electrification efforts have been held back in part by dated infrastructure and a grid system divided among regional operators.

While growing energy needs for artificial intelligence could spur upgrades, the United States is also seeing slow uptake of electric vehicles, after Congress repealed tax credits for new buyers. E. V.s account for less than 10 percent of new car sales in the United States, compared with more than 50 percent in China.

Taylor Rogers, a White House spokeswoman, said that the United States was focused on “common sense, not climate nonsense.”

“The Trump administration will continue to work with our allies around the world to unleash affordable, reliable, secure energy sources, all while driving energy addition,” she said.

The United States under President Trump has withdrawn from the Paris climate agreement and did not send a delegation to COP31, which includes more than 190 countries.

At the talks, organizers are trying to win support for a pledge to increase the electrification rate by 2035 to 35 percent, compared with the current 23 percent. The target was initially designed as a voluntary sign-up measure, and it’s been backed by more than two dozen countries, including Pakistan and Britain, as well as the European Union.

But as the conference heads into its final days, organizers are also hoping to include the pledge in a final agreement that would require consensus. As a result, the electrification issue has become a magnet for the other, longstanding climate fights over funding and fossil fuels. Some nations want clear language that electrification should go hand-in-hand with renewables. The leader of a negotiating bloc representing 44 lower-income nations said its support hinged on financing that could make electricity gains more feasible.

“We need money and technology,” said Adão Soares Barbosa, a negotiator from East Timor who heads the group.

China has not formally backed the electrification pledge. The Chinese delegation at COP31 did not respond to a request for comment. Mr. Li, of the Asia Society, said that China did not see the utility of setting new global targets. But he also predicted that China would not object.

He noted that China is aiming to hit the 35 percent electrification mark by 2030, five years ahead of the global target.

“Look, this target will not make them sweat,” he said.

item.title: Trump’s plan for A.I. supremacy fuels resistance in the Philippines.
item.description:
In May, Roseller Rodriguez, a mayor in the Philippines, was startled to learn from news reports that U.S. officials had arrived in his district to start an artificial intelligence hub.

He saw a video of senior American and Filipino officials standing on a makeshift stage, unveiling a new initiative called Pax Silica.

Mr. Rodriguez had not been invited. Nor had he ever heard about the hub. Was it a data center? Where would the water and electricity come from? What would happen to the farmers living there?

Months later, he says he has few answers.

“I’m not concerned with the geopolitics of Pax Silica,” Mr. Rodriguez said in his office in the municipality of Capas. “My problem is Pax Silica will be built in our community.”

The United States started Pax Silica to unite partners around A.I. supply chains independent of China. The initiative is part of President Trump’s effort to counter Beijing’s economic and technological influence.

Trump administration officials have cast it as a 21st-century successor to Pax Americana, the era of relative peace among major powers after World War II.

The significance of Pax Silica, which 26 signatories have joined, has become heightened after revelations that Nvidia’s former chief executive, Jensen Huang, was targeted by Chinese intelligence, exposing the growing geopolitical stakes of the global A.I. race.

In the Philippines, America’s oldest ally in Asia, the backlash has been fierce.

item.title: What are APEC, ASEAN and the Quad?
item.description:
President Trump landed in Manila on Tuesday, beginning a trip to Asia in which he will attend an ASEAN summit, greet members of the Quad, then travel to China for an APEC meeting.

Here’s what those acronyms mean, as well as some highlights from previous summits — including gold crowns and awkward handshakes.

The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum is a group of 21 member economies, most of which are from that region. Its members also include Canada, Mexico, Australia, Russia and the United States. It promotes trade in Asia, but is not a free trade bloc. Its leaders meet annually, with the location rotating each year.

Meetings between world leaders on the sidelines of the summit can often overshadow the main proceedings. This year, in the Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen, Mr. Trump is expected to meet with President Xi Jinping of China and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia, as well as with Mr. Xi separately.

Last year, when Mr. Trump visited the South Korean city of Gyeongju during the week of the APEC meeting, President Lee Jae Myung of South Korea gave him a replica of a gold crown that researchers believe was worn by an ancient Korean ruler. Mr. Trump also met with Mr. Xi in the nearby city of Busan, where the two struck a truce in their countries’ trade war.

A notable incident happened in Sydney, Australia, in 2007, when a group of local television comedians brought an Osama bin Laden look-alike through security. The team came within yards of a hotel where President George W. Bush was staying.

The Association of Southeast Asian Nations is a grouping of 11 countries — Brunei, Cambodia, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Myanmar, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, East Timor and Vietnam — which promotes political cooperation and stability across the region. Its leaders meet twice annually.

The bloc was formed in 1967 and represents nearly 700 million people. Its economy and its role in global markets have strengthened in recent years. The United States also sees ASEAN as a geostrategic bulwark against China.

In 2009, an ASEAN meeting in Thailand fell into acrimony when Secretary of State Hillary Clinton compared North Korea’s leaders to “small children” when discussing their nuclear program. The country’s leadership, in turn, described Ms. Clinton as a “schoolgirl” and a “pensioner.”

During the 2017 ASEAN summit in Manila, Mr. Trump grimaced while jostling with Southeast Asian leaders for an awkward cross-armed handshake that was captured in a group photograph.

The Quadrilateral Security Dialogue is an informal partnership between Australia, India, Japan and the United States, which was formed in part to counter China. It was proposed by Prime Minister Shinzo Abe of Japan in 2007.

Beijing opposed the initial discussion, lodging formal diplomatic protests. Australia withdrew in 2008 and the dialogue was put on hold for some time. But the grouping was revived in 2017 on the sidelines of an ASEAN conference.

President Biden was the first U.S. president to convene a meeting among the leaders of the nations as a foursome. In 2024, he hosted the Quad leaders at his home in Wilmington, Del. Mr. Trump has appeared to be less enthusiastic about the partnership. Last year, he did not attend the Quad summit in India.

item.title: Young Filipinos Protest Trump and Marcos Before They Meet
item.description:
Several hundred activists massed on Tuesday in central Manila to march to the Philippine International Convention Center, the venue for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit.

By the time President Trump landed in the city, the ranks of the protesters had swelled to thousands.

Most of the demonstrators were university students who said that they were fed up with the government, which they said was more focused on preserving its relationship with the United States than helping impoverished Filipinos.

Cinna Sison, 18, who studies European languages at the University of the Philippines, said they were inspired by the recent mass protests in France.

“I love the French,” she said. “They know how to protest.

Ms. Sison said she had worn colorful makeup to mark her first time attending a demonstration. “I am here to show my solidarity with fellow young activists. We are here to show our disgust to the fascist Trump and to Marcos for kowtowing to his every wish,” she said, referring to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. of the Philippines.

Mr. Trump is expected to hold a bilateral meeting with Mr. Marcos on Wednesday before he heads to China for an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.

The Philippine president, who earlier this year described Washington as a “steadfast partner,” has said little publicly about meeting Mr. Trump. His administration has hinted that the two sides are working on a military aid agreement.

In Manila, Ms. Sison wore a red scarf on her head and a red shirt with the words “Silicone not Silica” — a reference to Pax Silica, a U.S.-led consortium of countries aiming to create artificial intelligence supply chains independent of China.

Ms. Sison added that Pax Silica was a symbolic return of the Americans to the Philippines, the site of former U.S. military bases, as Washington leaned on a regional ally to counter China.

“Neighborliness is important, but it is not important to be subservient to U.S. interests,” she said.

Nearby, Raja Bausing, a 22-year-old visual artist, was busy putting the finishing touches on a papier-mâché model of Trump holding Marcos.

“We want to show how Trump is a warmonger, while Marcos is a lap dog,” she said. “They are very disrespectful to Filipinos. Trump was welcomed in a grand way and yet we Filipinos are maltreated.”

item.title: Trump’s ‘trade deal’ with Thailand is not a done deal.
item.description:
President Trump is expected to meet with Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul of Thailand on Tuesday in Manila to sign what the White House has described as a “trade deal.”

But Thailand’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement on Tuesday that Bangkok was expecting to agree only on a “joint statement marking progress in negotiations.”

The dissonance comes amid growing signs within ASEAN, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, that the United States is not a reliable partner. The meeting between Mr. Trump and Mr. Anutin is taking place on the sidelines of an ASEAN summit.

For more than a year, Washington and Bangkok have been negotiating a new trade agreement that covers items like tariffs, food imports and labor rights.

Last year, the United States battered Thailand with a 36 percent tariff, one of the steepest rates levied by Mr. Trump after his return to office. The United States is one of Thailand’s largest export markets, including for goods like pet food.

Mr. Trump later reduced the tariffs to 19 percent, before the U.S. Supreme Court struck them down in February. The administration eventually found a way to still impose 12.5 percent tariffs on Thai goods.

The signing of a U.S.-Thai trade deal might still be far off, requiring Thailand’s parliament to pass a law, but the meeting delivers an easy publicity win for Mr. Anutin and Mr. Trump, who is known to revel even in perceived success.

Pavida Pananond, an economist at Thammasat Business School in Bangkok, said, “The level of trust Thailand has in the U.S. is not at the same level as before all this economic weaponization of tariffs.”

item.title: Putin Is Open to Meeting With North Korea’s Leader in China, Kremlin Says
item.description:
President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia could meet with Kim Jong-un if the North Korean leader travels to China for the APEC summit this week, the Kremlin said, reflecting the deepening of ties between their countries in recent years.

Asked about the possibility of a meeting, Dmitri S. Peskov, the Kremlin spokesman, said on Monday that it would “of course” happen if Mr. Kim went to Shenzhen, the Chinese economic hub and host city, according to Russian state news agencies. North Korea has not confirmed whether Mr. Kim plans to attend the summit.

Mr. Putin and Mr. Kim have publicly met three times since 2022, and North Korea has been a key supporter of Russia’s military actions in Ukraine.

As the war in Ukraine nears its fifth anniversary, with no end in sight, the Kremlin is expected to use Mr. Putin’s many meetings at the APEC summit to showcase how Russia is regarded as one of the major international powers alongside the United States and China.

A visit by Mr. Kim would be a rare foray outside North Korea for the leader, and it would further raise the prospect that he could meet with President Trump in China. On the first day of his 48-hour trip to Asia, Mr. Trump told reporters that Mr. Kim “would like” to come to the APEC summit. The president has repeatedly said he would like to meet with Mr. Kim again.

On Wednesday, Mr. Putin is scheduled to meet with Xi Jinping, China’s leader. On Thursday, he is set to take part in a trilateral summit with Mr. Xi and Mr. Trump, the first meeting of its kind. The Kremlin said on Monday that it was working to arrange a bilateral meeting between Mr. Putin and Mr. Trump.

Before his departure for China, Mr. Putin met on Monday in the Kremlin with Jo Yong-won, a secretary of North Korea’s ruling Workers’ Party. During the meeting, Mr. Putin said that North Korea’s help in driving Ukrainian forces from the Kursk region of Russia last year “marked a new chapter in the history of military cooperation between our countries.”

Moscow planned to unveil a monument in Kursk by the end of the year to honor the North Korean troops, Mr. Putin said.

item.title: Anne Thurston Has Died. She Revealed Salacious Details of Mao’s Life.
item.description:
Anne F. Thurston, an American political scientist and expert on China who co-wrote a best-selling book with Mao Zedong’s longtime personal physician that revealed intimate — and often bawdy — details about the dictator’s personal life, died on Oct. 2 in Alexandria, Va. She was 83.

The death, at a senior-care facility, was from complications of dementia, said Adam Nelson, a longtime friend and colleague.

“The Private Life of Chairman Mao,” published in 1994 and co-written with Dr. Li Zhisui, was Dr. Thurston’s sole best seller, but she wrote, co-wrote or edited numerous books that, despite being academic in tone, were acclaimed studies of the individual experiences of Chinese people.

She often focused on dissidents of one kind or another and how their lives were upended during the transformations of Chinese society in the latter half of the 20th century, beginning with Mao’s decade-long campaign of persecution known as the Cultural Revolution.

David Lampton, the former director of the China program at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies in Washington, remembered choosing Dr. Thurston in 1999 as one of his first hires.

“Anne was one of the greatest and most credible contributors to our understanding of China,” he said. “Hers was a unique mixture of empathy and understanding about why China behaved the way it did, but it never slid into being an apologist. Her sympathy was with people on China’s periphery.”

Dr. Thurston was one of the first American political scientists to be granted research access to China during the thaw in U.S.-China relations after Mao’s death in 1976. After an initial visit three years later, Dr. Thurston spent much of her career going back and forth to China.

In a personal statement she wrote while working as a researcher at the Wilson Center in Washington, one of the think tanks, universities and other institutions with which she was affiliated over the decades, she said her mission was “to listen to Chinese people tell their stories — and then to relate those stories here in the West in a way that makes sense to both us and the storytellers themselves.”

Her trip to China in 1979 was a “turning point,” she wrote. The accounts of the Cultural Revolution relayed to her by Chinese counterparts in political science programs were “at such odds with the official, printed accounts,” she recalled, that she resolved to center her first published book on extensive field work with Chinese intellectuals.

Dozens of interviews, with private citizens and Chinese officials, resulted in what she considered her favorite of all her books, “Enemies of the People: The Ordeal of the Intellectuals in China’s Great Cultural Revolution” (1987).

Writing in The New York Times, the Sinologist Merle Goldman called the work “an important book because the victims believe that the more the outside world (as well as the Chinese) knows about what happened in the Cultural Revolution, the less likely it is that such a phenomenon may reoccur.” The Times included the volume on its list of the year’s notable books.

But it was Dr. Thurston’s third book, “The Private Life of Chairman Mao,” that received worldwide attention. It was a collaboration with Mao’s personal physician, Dr. Li, who kept journals while he cared for Mao for more than two decades, burned them because he feared retribution during the Cultural Revolution, and then recreated them from memory for the book.

She conducted extensive interviews with Dr. Li, who began living in the United States in 1988, followed by separate research to confirm details, and she basically wrote the book.

“The Private Life of Chairman Mao” was deemed so newsworthy that, soon before its official publication day, it merited a front-page article in The Times, although the reporter credited Dr. Thurston only once, in passing, as Dr. Li’s “editorial assistant.”

The Times review that followed, by the historian Marilyn B. Young of New York University, credited her correctly as the co-author and recounted the book’s descriptions of “Mao’s appetite for young women and fatty pork, his addiction to sleeping pills, his adherence to esoteric Taoist sexual practices, his reluctance to bathe or brush his teeth.”

The most intimate portrait of Mao ever released, it became an international best seller and was denounced by the Chinese government as slander. The authorities took issue with Dr. Li’s characterizations of how Mao’s tyrannical attitude led to disastrous policy choices, but the salacious details garnered much of the public’s attention.

Mao's sprawling sex life had been alluded to in other works, but the stories Dr. Li recounted in his book with Dr. Thurston spoke to a closeness to the man that others simply didn’t have.

Dr. Li recalled, for instance, how Mao had repeatedly sent him young women with symptoms of the protozoan parasite Trichomonas vaginalis, which is sexually transmitted. “The young women were proud to be infected,” he and Dr. Thurston wrote. “The illness, transmitted by Mao, was a badge of honor, testimony to their close relations with the Chairman.”

Anne Elizabeth Fritter, the older of two sisters, was born on July 16, 1943, in Manhattan. Her father was Lee W. Fritter, an Army colonel, and her mother was Aileene (O’Dea) Fritter.

She graduated in 1965 from Tufts University with a bachelor’s degree in government and received a master’s degree (1966) and a doctorate (1974), both in political science from the University of California, Berkeley.

Her marriages to Thom B. Thurston and Patrick G. Maddox ended in divorce. She is survived by a sister, Mary Fritter of Germantown, Md.

Later in her career, Dr. Thurston’s attention shifted to Tibet. For years, she directed the Grassroots China Initiative at the School of Advanced International Studies, often taking groups of researchers and students to Tibet. Beginning in 2012, Beijing refused her a visa, and she never returned to China.

In a tribute to her, Yawei Liu, the senior adviser on China to the Carter Center, another Washington think tank Dr. Thurston was affiliated with, said she was a “bridge between scholars and the public long before the concept of the public intellectual was coined.”

Moreover, he wrote, she exuded a sense of style and “no matter where she was or where she was going, she always dressed elegantly,” even in rural areas of Tibet.

Her final book, “The Noodle Maker of Kalimpong: the Dalai Lama’s Brother and His Struggle For Tibet” (2015), was co-written with Gyalo Thondup, the 14th Dalai Lama’s elder brother. It documented the story of Mr. Thondup’s decades as his family’s secret diplomatic middleman between officials in China, India and the United States.

Noel Millea contributed reporting.

item.title: President Trump Starts Asia Trip by Shrugging Off U.S. Concerns: ‘It’s Fine’
item.description:
President Trump arrived in Manila on Tuesday, at the tail end of a diplomatic summit in which world leaders had arranged to hold part of the gathering at his hotel. His agenda was supposed to be about inking trade deals and embracing regional partnerships, but several problems from home had followed him overseas.

He was pelted with questions. He seemed to meet each with a shrug.

Did he have any worries about the aviation-system meltdown afflicting travelers across the United States, or a technological outage affecting several large banking systems?

“It’s life,” Mr. Trump said. “When you’re big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen. It’s fine.”

What about news reports, so far unconfirmed by the Trump administration, that Iran may be thinking about how to unleash a dirty bomb in Washington? Was an attack on American soil imminent?

“I hope it’s not,” Mr. Trump said, not exactly the voice of reassurance. “But we take it very seriously. Because they happen to be crazy.”

Mr. Trump is not shy about prizing photo opportunities. But his appearance showcased just how little he seemed to be interested in netting diplomatic wins or easing concerns about American leadership — his leadership — as he made this quick stop at the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.

His appearance was on the way to the main event later in the week: a meeting on the edges of the APEC economic summit in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday with Presidents Xi Jinping of China and Vladimir V. Putin of Russia, two authoritarians whom Mr. Trump openly admires.

Mr. Trump will be meeting Mr. Xi for the third time this year, and there is another likely next month at Mr. Trump’s Doral resort in Miami, where he gets to play the host (and has invited Mr. Putin, ending the Russian leader’s isolation for invading Ukraine). The three-way meeting between China, Russia and the United States would be the first of its kind.

Mr. Trump’s visit to Manila amounted to a layover. When he arrived, he trudged off the plane like all weary long-haul travelers do, and slowly made his way down the stairs of Air Force One. Mr. Trump was then whisked to his hotel, where several world leaders had gathered to bring the diplomatic summit to his doorstep.

Alongside members of the so-called Quad — the informal grouping that includes the United States, India, Japan and Australia — his comments were brief, cryptic and nearly mechanical: “Quad is important. We’re working on things that will surprise people.”

On the way to Manila, Mr. Trump floated a meeting with another leader, Kim Jong Un, the North Korean leader and a dictator he has talked warmly about, perhaps in Shenzhen. It isn’t clear why he wants to see Mr. Kim: The three meetings he held in his first term ended in failure, and today the North has more nuclear weapons, and more ways to launch them, then ever before.

If he holds the meeting it would also surprise his staff. Last week, White House officials said that there was no chance of a Trump-Kim meeting. On Tuesday, the White House did not explain whether plans for such a meeting were taking shape.

Mr. Trump’s trip was planned before the midterm elections, but few Republicans, including Mr. Trump, had predicted them to be a near complete wipeout of the president’s handpicked candidates. His appearance in Asia, two weeks after the election, is in keeping with a long tradition of global trips taken by presidents hoping to divert attention from a damaging domestic story by flexing American power abroad.

In November 1994, days after Republicans took control of Congress for the first time in decades, President Bill Clinton departed for the Philippines. In 2010, after Democrats lost 63 House seats, President Barack Obama traveled through India, Indonesia, South Korea, Japan and Portugal. Mr. Trump even did it in his first term, jetting to France after Republicans lost control of the House in 2018.

This time, there was little of substance on Mr. Trump’s schedule aside from signing a trade deal between the United States and Thailand. In the end, not even the trade deal materialized, with the president saying that it would be finished in the coming weeks.

“I look forward to finalizing the details of our formal agreement in the coming weeks,” Mr. Trump said. “Our staff is working on it very diligently, and it’ll be done. But the concept of what we have will be really very permanent, and we’re just about there.” He signed something anyway, even in the absence of a deal, under the theory that no favorable photo should go unsnapped.

Several of the factors that made Mr. Trump an unpopular president at home have made him an increasingly unpredictable partner abroad. All three Quad partners are smarting from high energy prices triggered by the Iran war, a conflict Mr. Trump never discussed with them before launching it in late February. And Mr. Trump’s insistence that the United States must win the A.I. race against China has encountered pushback in the Philippines, where some Filipinos are vehemently opposed to Pax Silica, a project led by the U.S. government that would establish a technology hub about the size of 3,000 football fields.

During an address to Quad leaders on Tuesday evening, Mr. Trump again focused on personal relationships over policy. He called Prime Minister Narendra Modi of India, a member of the group, “a great leader and a friend of mine, highly respected by everybody all over the world.” The president also praised Mr. Modi as a “very tough man.” The countries are at odds over India’s purchases of Russian oil, and trade talks have dragged on, frustrating both parties.

Later, the Quad leaders issued a joint statement, affirming the group as “a force for good and a partnership of action, committed to peace, stability, and prosperity” and outlining several plans, including maritime flyovers of the Indo-Pacific, cooperation on combating cyberattacks, and accelerating work on A.I. initiatives.

Before ending his day, Mr. Trump delivered remarks at a dinner of ASEAN leaders, and praised his host, President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. of the Philippines.

“I don’t want to date myself, but I knew your parents very well. They were great,” Mr. Trump said. “I believe in genetics. They did a good job. You have very good genetics, I can tell you that.”

It was not the first time Mr. Trump has praised the family of Mr. Marcos, who is the son of the dictator Ferdinand E. Marcos, who ruled the Philippines for 20 years, imposed martial law, and was ousted in 1986.

On Wednesday, Mr. Trump will stay in Manila long enough to have lunch at Malacañang Palace and a bilateral meeting with Mr. Marcos before departing for Shenzhen.

In China, Mr. Trump needs to extend a soon-expiring trade truce that limited tariffs on Chinese goods entering the United States in return for a Chinese commitment not to cut off rare earths and magnets.

The president is also going to focus on the issue of nuclear proliferation in his meeting with Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin, though White House officials do not expect any significant breakthroughs.

Also lingering over Mr. Trump’s trip to Asia is the fallout from the resignation of Jensen Huang, the chief executive of the chip maker Nvidia, after revelations he had engaged in extramarital affairs, including with a woman whom U.S. officials have identified as a Chinese intelligence asset.

Mr. Huang has been influential in shaping the president’s views about technological competition with China, and made the argument that keeping China dependent on American-made semiconductor chips and technology could help maintain U.S. dominance over Beijing.

Mr. Huang’s resignation — and the approach the Commerce Department took to slowing rules that would clamp down on the sale of Nvidia chips to overseas data centers — has exposed a long-burning feud within the Trump administration. Howard Lutnick, the commerce secretary, who has argued for less strict limits on chip exports to Asia, joined Mr. Trump for the trip, as did Scott Bessent, the Treasury secretary, who in recent days publicly blamed the Commerce Department for failing to clamp down on the sale of advanced Nvidia technology.

Before leaving for Manila, Mr. Trump did not seem concerned about the scandal that has rocked a corporate juggernaut that is critical to the A.I. industry. His usual retort when asked about spying is that everyone does it, and he did not seem especially perturbed. If he was, he would not show it.

“You know, we’re heading to China, and I don’t think you want to insult China just before you get there,” Mr. Trump said.

Verena Hölzl and Suhasini Raj contributed reporting.
