item.title: Nabeel Rajab, Renowned Bahraini Human Rights Activist, Dies at 62
item.description:
Nabeel Rajab, a Bahraini human rights activist who spent decades fighting for greater political freedoms in his authoritarian home country, often from behind prison bars, died on Tuesday in Istanbul. He was 62.

Family members found Mr. Rajab motionless on Tuesday morning, and paramedics were unable to revive him, said Ebrahim Sharif, a friend and fellow Bahraini activist who spoke with Mr. Rajab’s family after his death. Family members believe he had a heart attack, he said.

Mr. Rajab played a key role in the pro-democracy uprising that swept Bahrain in 2011 during the Arab Spring, before protests were violently crushed by the government. He was well known and respected far beyond the borders of Bahrain, an island nation in the Persian Gulf.

In 2013, he was one of several Bahraini activists who were awarded Norway’s prestigious Rafto Prize “for their long and courageous fight for fundamental human rights.”

Mr. Rajab was arrested by the Bahraini authorities numerous times, spending more than six years in prison on charges related to his activism and his criticism of authoritarian Arab governments. He continued his work from inside prison, connecting with fellow inmates and urging Western powers to stand up to the government of Bahrain, a close U.S. ally.

“Only democracy can bring stability to the Middle East,” he wrote in 2015 in a letter from jail to President Barack Obama. “And while democracy may take time to develop, the process cannot begin unless our right to free speech is protected.”

Mr. Rajab stayed in Bahrain for years, even as political repression deepened there.

He finally went into exile earlier this year, after speaking publicly about the apparent torture of Sayed Mohammed al-Mousawi, a young Bahraini man who died in custody, said Sayed Ahmed Alwadaei, a Bahraini activist based in Britain.

“The legacy Nabeel left behind is incredibly rich,” said Khalid Ibrahim, head of the Gulf Center for Human Rights, which is based in Lebanon. “He chose to live in exile rather than submit to the oppression of tyrants, and throughout his life, he never feared confronting them.”

Born in 1964, Mr. Rajab attended college in India before returning home.

In Bahrain, a Shiite Muslim-majority country ruled by a Sunni Muslim royal family, Shiite citizens have long complained of repression and marginalization. The country has a history of protest and activism, and Mr. Rajab became an important figure in those movements.

In 2000, he co-founded the Bahrain Human Rights Society. In 2011, he was one of several leaders of Bahrain’s Arab Spring uprising, when both Sunni and Shiite Bahrainis took to the streets to call for change.

After the government cracked down on their movement, Mr. Rajab continued to speak out for human rights, defending colleagues and friends who had been jailed.

“He was our voice outside the prison,” said Mr. Sharif, who was detained at that time. “He was the most courageous person who led demonstrations and sitdowns, and led the international campaign for our release.”

Mr. Rajab’s most recent arrest was in 2016, after he criticized the role of Bahrain, Saudi Arabia and the United States in the devastating war in Yemen. Bahraini authorities accused him of spreading false rumors in a time of war, insulting public authorities and insulting a foreign country. He was released in 2020.

Throughout his life, Mr. Rajab frequently called out Western powers for their close alliances with authoritarian Gulf Arab monarchs. He and many other Arab activists viewed these relations as hypocritical.

“Is this the kind of ally America wants?” he wrote in an opinion article in The New York Times in 2017. “The kind that punishes its people for thinking, that prevents its citizens from exercising their basic rights?”

Hadeel Buqrais, a Kuwaiti activist, said that Mr. Rajab was “one of the most significant pillars of human rights” in the region. “I doubt that anyone else could replicate what he achieved during such critical times,” she said.

”Despite all the suffering he endured, he remained cheerful, always smiling with hope and instilling that same hope in us,” she added. “He held a firm, unshakable belief that all these hardships would eventually pass.”

Outside of his work, Mr. Rajab was a funny and personable man who was able to build connections across religious, economic and political fault lines, Mr. Sharif said.

Mahmoud AlMousawi, a friend who met Mr. Rajab in college in India, described him as “a human rights advocate in the truest sense, one who sought neither position nor fame.”

“At his core, he could not tolerate the oppression, degradation or belittlement of any human being,” Mr. AlMousawi said. “He stood by his fellow human beings until his very last breath, without ever making distinctions based on religion, skin color, race, gender or nationality.”

Mr. Rajab is survived by his wife and two children.

item.title: Trump Won’t Just Be Late to a Southeast Asia Summit. He’ll Be Really Late.
item.description:
For the second year in a row, President Trump is attending the annual gathering of Southeast Asian leaders, a show of alliance to a region that the United States sees as a strategic and maritime counterweight to China.

But Mr. Trump will reach the gathering, held this year in Manila, only on Tuesday, just as the summit wraps up, and he is not expected to make any significant policies or diplomacy moves.

Mixed signals like this — to say nothing of Mr. Trump’s punishing tariffs — are adding to a widespread belief within ASEAN, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, that the United States is not a reliable partner. That leaves the bloc balancing between Washington and Beijing, with which many of its members have deep trade partnerships.

“They’ve learned that the United States is not reliable, so a lot of the hedging has been away from the United States,” said Ted Osius, a former U.S. ambassador to Vietnam.

The Philippines, America’s oldest security ally in Asia, provides a window into this balancing act.

After taking office three years ago, President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. reversed his predecessor’s tilt toward China and pivoted back toward the United States. That stance contributed to many tense encounters between Filipino and Chinese vessels in the South China Sea, where Manila and Beijing have competing territorial claims.

As U.S. patrols in the South China Sea have dropped, Mr. Marcos has appeared to be more conciliatory toward Beijing. In August, he said that there was a “distinct possibility” that the Philippines and China could partner on oil and gas exploration in those waters despite their territorial feud.

“Marcos Jr. already has begun a shift toward China, one that a single visit by Trump is unlikely to stop,” Joshua Kurlantzick, a senior fellow for Southeast Asia and South Asia at the Council on Foreign Relations, wrote last week.

On Sunday, China and ASEAN failed to agree on a code of conduct in the South China Sea — something the Philippines, which has some of the biggest stakes in the dispute, had vowed to secure while chairing the bloc this year.

Chester Cabalza, president of International Development and Security Cooperation, a Philippine think tank, said, “Strategically, Manila opens its doors for conciliation with Beijing to stabilize normal ties. But on the ground, the real battle has yet to subside.”

Domestically, Mr. Marcos has to walk a tightrope, too.

“For Filipino fishermen and coastal communities, the South China Sea is not simply about a geopolitical dispute. It concerns livelihoods, access to maritime resources and national dignity,” said Arnaud Leveau, president of the Asia Centre, a Paris-based think tank. Any diplomatic accommodation perceived as sacrificing Filipino interests, he said, would therefore be politically risky.

The wider region has been battered by the consequences of another Trump policy: the war in Iran. Southeast Asia depends heavily on oil and gas imports from the Middle East and was roiled by soaring prices of fuel. In the Philippines, crops rotted in fields because farmers could not afford to transport them to markets. In Thailand, public servants were asked to use stairs instead of elevators to reduce energy expenses.

ASEAN comprises 11 nations — Brunei, Cambodia, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Myanmar, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, Vietnam, and, since last year, East Timor — with vastly different degrees of freedom and wealth. The bloc represents almost 700 million people, or almost 10 percent of the global population.

Making decisions on a consensus-basis and pledging not to interfere in one other’s internal affairs, the bloc has often been criticized as slow and ineffective, with the situation in Myanmar often cited as an example. A coup in that country in 2021 unleashed a civil war that ranks among the world’s most violent conflicts.

Myanmar’s leaders remain barred from ASEAN summits, under an agreement that was extended on Monday. Still, almost half of the bloc’s member states have had bilateral engagements with Myanmar since the coup leader, Min Aung Hlaing, used stage-managed elections to take the post of president this year. Washington has also recently re-engaged in direct talks with Myanmar.

Mr. Trump’s attendance at the summit, which concludes with an ASEAN-U.S. meeting, is part of a state visit to the Philippines. He is expected to hold a bilateral meeting with Mr. Marcos on Wednesday before heading to China for an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. Mr. Marcos has said little publicly about meeting Mr. Trump; but earlier this year, he described Washington as a “steadfast partner.” His administration has hinted that the two sides are working on a military aid agreement.

In recent days, hundreds of demonstrators have gathered in Manila to protest Mr. Trump’s visit. They oppose his “Pax Silica” initiative, a move to build a supply chain for the artificial intelligence industry that bypasses China, saying it would exploit Philippine natural resources.

Renato Reyes, who led one of the protest groups on Sunday afternoon, said, “Marcos is so desperate to welcome Donald Trump that he will roll out the red carpet, even if Trump arrives late for the summit.”

Aie Balagtas See contributed reporting from Manila and Damien Cave from Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam.

item.title: They’re Young, Frustrated and Want France to Change. They Disagree on How.
item.description:
Soumaya Sarré, 18, is a history and Arabic studies undergraduate who grew up in a working-class district on the edge of Paris. She is a voice of the youth-led protests that have spurred unrest across France since September. “I can carry our voices, the voices of young people from working-class neighborhoods,” she told me.

Louise Montangon, 22, is a philosophy undergraduate from rural France. As the student protests gained momentum, she became one of their leading critics, regularly condemning the young demonstrators on television panels and social media. “The majority of university and high school students actually want to attend their classes,” she said in an interview.

Unknown to the public until this fall, these two women from opposite ends of the political spectrum have surfaced as emblems of the combustible French moment, which was set to intensify again on Tuesday with more strikes and protests.

Ms. Sarré and Ms. Montangon aren’t formal leaders of their political camps, and their sudden prominence partly reflects society’s tendency to search for avatars for leaderless movements. Their simultaneous rise, and their divergent politics, nevertheless reflect the polarization of French society, and particularly its youth — five months from a presidential election dominated by candidates from the far-left and the far-right.

Polls of people under 25 suggest that more than 40 percent support the main far-left candidate, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, while more than 20 percent back his far-right opponent, Marine Le Pen. In legislative elections in 2024, nearly half of voters from that age group voted for Mr. Mélenchon’s party, and a third voted for Ms. Le Pen’s.

Support for moderate solutions has plummeted after years of centrist governance under Emmanuel Macron, France’s term-limited president.

Mr. Macron took steps that helped to reduce unemployment, while on the international stage he successfully led a push for Europe to take more responsibility for its own security. Yet his administration has struggled to revive France’s economy and its institutions, including its education system — spurring street unrest and leaving the country on the verge of a debt crisis.

Ms. Sarré and Ms. Montangon embody a French society that is increasingly reaching for maximalist answers to those problems — but divided on how to solve them.

They agree on the main problems that ignited the student protests: the dilapidated state of French schools, teacher shortages, and an opaque university application system. And they are both furious with Mr. Macron and his allies.

“Seriously, Macron, you’re pushing it!” Ms. Sarré said in a selfie video in late September that marked her rise toward wider prominence. She railed against government policies that she said focused more on banning Muslim clothing — like her hijab — from schools, rather than on improving the education system.

Ms. Montangon won national attention 10 days later, on Oct. 6, when she joined a televised debate with Gabriel Attal, one of Mr. Macron’s former prime ministers and a candidate in the presidential race.

“There’s no point in looking at me with a little smile — your track record is disastrous,” Ms. Montangon told the politician in a self-assured tone, pointing to France’s decline in academic rankings. “You’re the face of permissiveness,” she added.

She and Ms. Sarré diverge over where France should go next.

“It’s possible to make our voice heard without breaking everything, without blocking everything,” Ms. Montangon said.

In a separate interview, Ms. Sarré disagreed. The protests should last “as long as there is no concrete change,” she said.

Ms. Sarré’s left-wing politics were forged in Bondy, a town north of Paris with an unusually large number of immigrants, and high rates of poverty and unemployment.

She is the child of a Senegalese father who works in the civil service and a French mother, who is currently unemployed. She studied at a high school called Jean Renoir, where, she said, buildings were so poorly insulated that students would keep their coats on as they studied in classrooms with peeling walls, broken chairs and ill-functioning computers.

During her senior year in 2026, Jean Renoir made headlines when an adviser at the school was suspended after being accused of racism toward a student. The experience inspired Ms. Sarré to help lead an antiracist student movement. The school administration and the education ministry, which oversees the school, did not reply to a request for comment.

Ms. Sarré, like other students from the edge of Paris, also struggled with her university application. Despite her stellar grades, Ms. Sarré said, she was not immediately accepted to her first-choice program. “So, if I, with that academic record, found it this difficult to get into university, I knew it was even worse for everyone else,” she said.

She empathized with the demands of other students who had begun blockading their schools in September. She attended their protests, organized solidarity demonstrations and helped create a union, which she now leads, for students in working-class neighborhoods.

Ms. Montangon said she was raised in a single-parent household in a small village in western France, though she declined to name it for fear of retribution against her family. She recalled a similar high school experience to Ms. Sarré’s: overcrowded classrooms, badly insulated buildings.

In her teens, she said, she even leaned left and admired Mr. Mélenchon, the far-left leader.

Ms. Montangon’s conservative politics took shape at 18, after she started her bachelor’s degree in Bordeaux. Her experience in what she described as “an extremely politicized university” changed her mind.

“There’s pressure on students who don’t want to join the various left-wing and far-left groups,” she said. “There’s pressure on professors who don’t want their classes disrupted by activists” from left-wing backgrounds.

Ms. Montangon soon joined a right-wing student union of university students, and later the National Rally, Ms. Le Pen’s party.

As student demonstrations spread across France in September, she said she decided that nothing justified the disruption they caused.

Though she agreed with left-wing calls for more investment in public education, she decided that the far-right’s emphasis on law and order was more likely to bring about national stability.

The National Rally, she said, “advocates common sense and a return to order in a society that’s going through a lot right now.”

Since September, Ms. Sarré and Ms. Montangon have been among roughly a dozen young people catapulted into the national spotlight by the French news media.

Problematically, experts say, none of those people — including Ms. Sarré and Ms. Montangon — are still high school students, undermining the idea that they speak for a generation.

“The fact that the media has focused on just a few people and had them appear on every talk show says nothing about those people, but it says a lot about the French media landscape,” said Fabien Truong, a sociologist who specializes in working-class districts.

Ms. Sarré’s Instagram following has jumped from 200 to more than 8,000, perhaps, she said, because it is “rare to see someone from a working-class neighborhood who expresses themselves well, who knows what they’re talking about, and is capable of defending their positions.”

Ms. Montangon has attracted more attention — her Instagram following has increased from 3,800 to roughly 280,000 — as she lashed out at protester violence, and at politicians whom she accuses of manipulating the movement.

Both have faced frequent abuse.

Ms. Sarré shared screenshots of comments on her videos that told her to “return to her country” — Ms. Sarré is French — and to take off her Muslim head scarf.

Ms. Montangon also shared screenshots of abuse she had received and said she had also been doxxed, and that her family had received death threats. She declined to provide certain details about her background for fear of retribution.

Neither plan on letting go of their newfound platform.

Ms. Sarré wants to keep going because the government’s response to the students has so far been unsatisfactory, she said. Its recent promise to overhaul the university admission program feels like a change in form, not substance, she said, and its new pledge to fund school renovations doesn’t go far enough.

Ms. Montangon sees this as a moment to galvanize a bloc of young right-leaning voters who are turned off by their peers’ protests.

“We are awakening a genuine patriotic, right-wing youth movement within universities and high schools,” Ms. Montangon said.

She wants her right-wing student union to be allowed to join negotiations between the government and youth representatives.

For now, that’s impossible. In an embodiment of France’s polarization, the left-leaning negotiators boycott any meeting that their right-wing counterparts want to join.

item.title: Leaked Files Show Deutsche Bank Protected Russian Profits Despite Warnings
item.description:
When Russian missiles began pummeling Ukraine in February 2022, executives at one of the world’s largest banks sensed trouble headed their way.

Within hours of an invasion that set off a war that is now in its fifth year, Western governments issued new financial sanctions intended to further isolate Russia from the world economy.

At Deutsche Bank, a longtime bank of Russian industry titans and oligarchs, officials scrambled to get ahead of the damage. “Russian Sanctions Urgent Request” read the subject line of an email sent by one of Deutsche’s anti-financial crime specialists to her colleagues.

“As you know we have a large Russian Oligarchs client population” and other clients with investments in Russian companies, she wrote. She asked which of those clients “we potentially could unwind and which not.” Should the bank advise them, she wondered, to withdraw their money “while they still can?”

This email exchange was the beginning of a frenzied reckoning within the scandal-plagued bank over its long resistance to breaking with Russia’s most important business titans under Vladimir V. Putin, the Russian president. The bank’s clients included the Russian billionaires Oleg V. Deripaska and Viktor F. Vekselberg. Time and again over many years, records show, Deutsche Bank’s risk managers warned that such relationships were perilous.

But profits associated with maintaining its Russian clients won out every time.

Russia’s war in Ukraine swept up Deutsche Bank in a larger shift. For decades, German politicians and business leaders believed that working with Russia and deepening economic ties between the two countries would discourage Russian aggression. That strategy collapsed after the invasion.

Deutsche Bank’s response to the sanctions, as well as new details about its long history with Russian clients, emerged from more than 15 million internal records, including confidential reports, emails and meeting minutes. The leaked records were obtained by the Indian author and journalist Josy Joseph and the South African journalist Khadija Sharife and were analyzed by a consortium of more than 200 journalists, including reporters for The New York Times.

The records provide a rare insider narration of Deutsche Bank’s yearslong cultivation of Russian oligarch clients. Those relationships continued even as units within the bank argued that handling the oligarchs’ finances put the bank at risk of inadvertently facilitating financial crimes.

That would be familiar turf for Deutsche. The fallout from Russia’s invasion capped a seven-year period during which Deutsche paid billions of dollars to settle claims by regulators that it had handled transactions for international bribery and money laundering, among other accusations. One of those cases involved the bank’s activities in Russia.

Even with its activities in Russia under scrutiny, Deutsche’s bankers debated how much they were obligated to tell the Justice Department about their Russian clients, records show. And bank executives initially resisted calls to exit the Russian market after the invasion. Only when competitors announced they would depart the Russian market did the bank finally pull up stakes.

Deutsche Bank, in recent written statements responding to questions for this article, said it had acted lawfully and never helped clients evade financial sanctions. “Following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, Deutsche Bank acted promptly to implement the rapidly evolving sanctions imposed by the relevant authorities,” the bank said.

For Russia’s politically connected ultrarich, Western financial houses like Deutsche Bank were essential. Deutsche Bank gave them the ability to do business in stable currencies and to keep their fortunes immune from Russia’s unpredictable economy and politics. Western bank accounts allowed oligarchs to buy professional sports teams and London mansions.

For years, experts have published research and given testimony before Congress showing that the Kremlin has used oligarchs as an instrument of soft power.

The newly obtained internal reports and emails capture the beginning of the end of Deutsche Bank’s long pursuit of Russian money.

After more than a century of an on-again-off-again presence in Russia, Deutsche Bank had become so ingrained there by 2008 that Mr. Putin spoke glowingly of the bank and personally met with Josef Ackermann, then the chief executive, in Moscow.

“The bank serves as a bridge between the Russian and German economies,” Mr. Putin said during the meeting.

Deutsche Bank had built a substantial clientele of oligarchs, the businesspeople who turned Kremlin connections into riches when state resources were parceled out after the fall of the Soviet Union.

Inside Deutsche Bank, some sounded warnings about these relationships — starting what would become a secret but defining pattern over the next decade and a half.

In 2014, the bank’s internal committee on reputational risk ranked its oligarch clients by the potential danger each posed to the bank’s image. At the top of the list was Mr. Deripaska, whose business interests have long intersected with the Kremlin’s and who has been called “Putin’s oligarch.”

An internal report noted that Mr. Deripaska had faced numerous allegations, including of money laundering in Spain, an ongoing tax evasion case, using the courts to “bully his competitors,” and having links to organized crime in Russia. Mr. Deripaska did not respond to questions seeking comment but previously said that he had been unfairly targeted for sanctions.

A bank division charged with insulating Deutsche from potential financial crimes raised similar concerns. Given the “frequency and seriousness of adverse information” about Mr. Deripaska, this report recommended “exiting those relationships where Deripaska is the controlling party.”

Elsewhere in the bank, in divisions focused on generating revenue, people offered a completely different take.

“Deutsche Bank has a longstanding business relationship with Mr. Deripaska,” one report read. “He is a reputable businessman and well-established business partner with a significant pipeline of further transactions.”

That argument won out, as it would for years to come.

An internal presentation from 2015 said, “Russian billionaires contribute heavily to our success.” Those well-heeled clients were considered the “backbone of sustainable growth” for the wealth-management division, a profitable segment for the bank.

A chart from that period showed that only four countries had more households than Russia with a net worth of at least $100 million, making it “an attractive market for wealth managers.”

Around that time, Deutsche entered a long period of regulatory and law enforcement challenges. The bank paid billions of dollars to settle allegations that it had manipulated interest rates in London, handled billions of dollars in transactions for clients in countries under U.S. sanctions and contributed to the 2008 financial crisis by pushing toxic mortgages on investors.

One of those cases, the “mirror trading” scandal, focused on Deutsche’s activities in Russia. Regulators in the United States and Britain accused Deutsche of helping Russian investors launder as much as $10 billion. Deutsche paid hundreds of millions of dollars in 2017 to settle the case.

In the aftermath, Deutsche dropped some of its clients and focused instead on the wealthiest Russians, which generally meant oligarchs.

“Russia is and will continue to be one of the most attractive and significant markets for Deutsche Bank in Europe,” said a statement announcing the appointment of Borislav Ivanov as the bank’s top executive in Russia.

As Deutsche embraced oligarchs, ties between the United States and Russia were growing strained.

In 2018, Steven T. Mnuchin, then the U.S. treasury secretary, accused Russia’s government and its oligarchs of fostering “malign activity around the globe.” He cited Russia’s invasion of Ukraine’s Crimea region and its meddling in the 2016 U.S. presidential election. The Trump administration placed financial sanctions on seven wealthy industrialists close to Mr. Putin.

Of them, five were Deutsche Bank clients, either personally or through business affiliations, internal records show.

The list included Mr. Deripaska, who remained a client despite earlier reservations. It also named Mr. Vekselberg and the investment company he had founded, Renova Group. Mr. Ackermann, who was by then Deutsche Bank’s chairman, also sat on the board of Renova. (Mr. Vekselberg has said he was unfairly targeted for economic sanctions.)

During a meeting of the Deutsche supervisory board’s risk committee in 2019, one adviser questioned keeping the oligarchs as clients given the increasing risk, according to minutes of the meeting.

“If one of the clients turns out to be bad,” the adviser said, “the loss will be a multiple of the return.”

Deutsche’s regulatory problems pushed open the bank’s doors to outside scrutiny. The bank had been subject to outside monitoring by the United States since the mirror-trading scandal. A 2020 settlement over the bank’s relationship with Jeffrey Epstein, the convicted sex offender, and its connection to a bank involved in a major Russian money laundering scheme extended that oversight. The monitors soon zeroed in on the oligarch clients.

A document from the leaked trove shows that in September 2020, outside lawyers hired by the State of New York recommended that Deutsche Bank “strongly consider” shutting down all “operations and service related to Russia at this time.”

A lawyer representing Deutsche noted in an email to bank executives that the monitor said many other banks had already “exited Russia or significantly downsized Russian operations.”

“Is this accurate?” the lawyer asked. “Are we in line with, ahead of, or behind our peers?”

Mr. Ivanov, Deutsche Bank’s top executive in Russia, took exception, replying that a competitor was still in Russia and “5x our size” in several lines of business.

That claim cannot be verified based on public records. But Deutsche’s records show that its ties to wealthy Russians continued.

In 2018, a Deutsche Bank executive emailed a colleague to say that she had just been in Luxembourg and noticed the bank was “significantly expanding” its Russian clientele there.

She added that when she had met with Luxembourg’s financial regulators, “the first thing they mentioned was their concern related to those Russian clients.”

Deutsche had been quietly moving its oligarch accounts to its offices in Luxembourg and Switzerland, countries with strict bank-secrecy laws. That could give the bank legal cover to deny government requests for client records, though this was never stated as a motivation for the change.

Deutsche Bank, in one of its recent statements to reporters, said it concentrated its wealth-management clients in those locations, not just the Russians, following industry practices. The bank said all its Russian clients were subject to applicable vetting requirements.

In November 2020, a 172-page “Russia Strategy Review” noted that 17 Russian clients were on what was known as the U.S. Treasury Department’s “Kremlin list” of 210 senior government officials and oligarchs. Only a few accounts remained based in Frankfurt, where Deutsche Bank has its headquarters, and they were being moved. It noted Russia’s “elevated” risk for money laundering and sanctions — but also noted “the relevance and profitability of the Russian market.”

An internal review, code-named Project Oak, explored how Deutsche’s correspondent banks in Russia could pull it into problematic transactions involving wealthy clients. Yet spreadsheets attached to internal emails in 2021 showed the bank still planning to expand its oligarch clientele.

One spreadsheet said Deutsche’s relationship with Alfa-Bank, Russia’s largest private commercial bank, was dormant “in principle” because of “technical issues” that “will be solved immediately.”

Regarding several business accounts linked to Mr. Vekselberg, the sheets noted that the bank’s anti-financial-crime division in Switzerland wanted to “exit the whole client relationship.” Employees elsewhere in the bank had concluded “that this is not possible at the moment.”

By then, Mr. Vekselberg had been under U.S. sanctions for years. His $100 million yacht had been seized by the Spanish and U.S. authorities in Mallorca. Mr. Deripaska also remained a client.

Yet again, Deutsche hung on.

In April 2021, Deutsche’s management board unanimously voted to pursue careful growth in Moscow, citing improvements to its internal controls. A draft of a report presented to the board cited the “relevance and profitability of the Russian market.”

“DB remains comfortable with its current presence and business model” in Russia, the draft report noted.

That comfort level quickly dissipated after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

In a flurry of emails, one executive wrote that new sanctions would “have a significant operational impact on DB.” Another wrote that a unit within the bank was now considering “effectively disallowing business with Russian parties.”

The dozen sanction packages that arrived within three days of the war, one executive wrote, had created “unprecedented complexity” and a nearly “unmanageable situation.”

A more worrisome complication lurked, carrying the threat of criminal prosecution.

The year before the full-scale war started, Deutsche signed an agreement with the U.S. Justice Department to avoid prosecution on allegations that it had paid bribes, disguised as consulting agreements, to politically connected figures. The agreement allowed the Justice Department to demand answers from the bank for the next three years about people and companies under sanctions.

Days after the invasion, federal prosecutors invoked the agreement. They sought the names and account balances of Russian clients under sanctions as well as steps the bank was taking to monitor Russian money flows.

An internal bank email said the prosecutors stressed “that the Bank will be closely scrutinized and judged on whether it is responding quickly and accurately.”

Because Deutsche Bank had moved oligarch accounts to countries with strict secrecy laws years earlier, it had legal grounds to refuse to disclose details about those clients. Deutsche “is not permitted to disclose customer data from Switzerland and Luxembourg to the D.O.J. (banking secrecy),” one specialist wrote in an email.

The bank also appears to have withheld details about companies that were less than 50 percent owned by oligarchs under sanctions, as generally allowed by a Treasury Department rule. That appears to have exempted some of Mr. Deripaska’s holdings, among others. (The bank, in its response for this article, did not address what information it provided the Justice Department.)

Prosecutors apparently accepted Deutsche’s responses. The bank said that it fulfilled its obligations under its agreement with the U.S. government. The Justice Department did not respond to requests for comment from the consortium that reported this article.

By March 2022, sentiment in Germany had swung sharply. The government provided weapons to Ukraine, agreed to European sanctions against Russia and halted its undersea gas pipeline from Russia.

On March 10, Christian Sewing, Deutsche’s chief executive, told employees that the bank would end some, but not all, of its Russian business. “We are often asked why we are not withdrawing completely from Russia,” he wrote in an email. “The answer is that this would go against our values. We have clients who cannot exit Russia overnight. And, as far as we can, we will continue to also support them, too, at this difficult time.”

That same day, as public pressure mounted, JPMorgan Chase and Goldman Sachs said they would withdraw from Russia.

Then Mr. Sewing reversed course. The following day, Deutsche announced that it was winding down operations in the country it had long seen as important to its future.

“There won’t be any new business in Russia,” the statement said.

Additional reporting was contributed by Emma Prest, Sophia Stahl, Michael Suntinger, Anna Lauterjung, Maria Theresa Cruz, Karina Shedrofsky, Elizabeth Bratton, Olaf Storbeck, Dan McCrum and Lukas Kotkamp. The investigation was coordinated by Barracuda Media with technical support from the Data and Research Center in Germany.

item.title: Carney and Xi Announce Trade Pact Ahead of Asia Summit
item.description:
Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada and China’s leader, Xi Jinping, have struck an agreement to reduce some tariffs between their countries, a largely symbolic move that shows relations between the two countries are warming as Canada’s ties to the United States falter.

While the expanded trade between China and Canada resulting from the accord in the Chinese tech and financial hub Shenzhen will be modest, involving just $280 million in exports, the pact — as well as the seemingly amicable meeting — illustrates a contrast to Mr. Carney’s relationship with President Trump. Earlier this year, Mr. Carney said that the United States was “at war” with Canada after trade negotiations between the two countries collapsed in acrimony.

Talks are restarting between Canada and the United States but there is no indication that Washington will back away from key irritants including tariffs of up to 50 percent on Canadian autos, steel and aluminum.

Since entering politics last year, Mr. Carney has been traveling the world to diversify Canada’s economic and political ties away from the United States. Those efforts include current talks to make Canada the European Union’s first associate member and Mr. Carney’s second formal meeting this year with Mr. Xi.

“The stabilization of our bilateral trade arrangement is indicative of how we can work together more broadly, pragmatically, to solve problems,” Mr. Carney said at the start of the meeting with Mr. Xi on Tuesday.

He added that Canada is ahead of schedule with its goal of a 50 percent increase in exports to China by the end of the decade.

China and Canada were in a trade war after the Canadian government under Justin Trudeau, Canada’s former prime minister, followed the lead of the Biden administration and imposed a 100 percent tariff on Chinese-made electric vehicles. China responded with tariffs on a variety of Canadian products, particularly canola, an oil seed.

That dispute was largely resolved in January during the first formal meeting between Mr. Xi and Mr. Carney. China lifted its canola tariff after Canada agreed to allow a relatively small number of Chinese E.V.s into the country at a minimal tariff rate.

Before Tuesday’s meeting, Mr. Xi attempted to put the frosty relations firmly in the past, which were worsened by China’s arrest in 2018 of two Canadians in retaliation for Canada detaining a Chinese telecommunications executive under an extradition request from the United States.

“The development of Chinese-Canadian relations over the years has provided us with an important lesson,” Mr. Xi said at the start of the meeting. “We must respect each other, pursue equality and mutual benefit and seek common ground while setting aside differences.”

Tuesday’s announcement will largely eliminate tariffs on frozen Canadian pork and several seafoods. Both were caught up in China’s E.V. retaliation. Canada, in turn, will continue to suspend tariffs on some Chinese steel and aluminum products that were set to expire at the end of the year. It will also expand the list of products covered by the suspension.

A Canadian government document said that since March car plants in China have exported 16,211 vehicles to Canada under an annual quota of 49,000. Half of those autos, it said, are priced at under 35,000 Canadian dollars. It said that a second Chinese automaker has been given safety approval by Canada for its cars. That company, which the government will not name, plans to offer only cars that cost less than 35,000 dollars, Canada’s price limit target.

On Monday in Phnom Penh, Cambodia, Mr. Carney said that Canada will turn to China, Japan and Europe to save its auto industry if it is unable to eliminate Mr. Trump’s tariffs.

The meeting between Mr. Carney and Mr. Xi came ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, which is being held in Shenzhen later this week.

Since his address to the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland in January Mr. Carney has become something of a champion for nations with advanced economies that are not super powers — a group he calls “middle powers.”

But the main event of the APEC summit will be a meeting between Mr. Xi, Mr. Trump and Vladimir V. Putin of Russia.

When asked earlier in his Asia trip about the super power summit, Mr. Carney repeated Canada’s support for Ukraine following Russia’s invasion.

Canadian officials said they do not expect that Mr. Trump and Mr. Carney will meet in Shenzhen. Mr. Carney is also unlikely to meet Mr. Putin. He said over the weekend that he would not boycott a summit group photo including Mr. Putin, but only out of respect for China.

item.title: These Ukrainians Aren’t in Combat. But They Deal With War Every Day.
item.description:
Mykhailo Biliak has spent most of his life in the funeral business, and he no longer remembers how many graves he has dug. But he knows he has buried more than 1,200 soldiers in Lviv, in western Ukraine, since Russia started its full-scale war in 2022. “The worst day was six funerals,” said Mr. Biliak, 62.

Hundreds of miles to the east, in a basement near the front line, Daryna Boiko, a 32-year-old anesthesiologist, prepared to attach an IV drip to a soldier wounded by a drone. “It won’t be scary,” she assured him. “It was scary out there,” he replied. “It’s fine here.”

In Kyiv, the capital, Hanna Buraho, a 53-year-old psychotherapist, made tea after a session with a group of soldiers. More than 5,000 service members have been through her rehabilitation program, which uses horses. “When the war started, everyone rushed to help each other, and every person wanted to do something of their own, so this is my contribution,” Ms. Buraho said.

This Ukrainian doctor works near the front, trying to save wounded soldiers.

This man has buried more than 1,200 soldiers.

This therapist tries to help damaged veterans heal.

This forensic pathologist once helped to solve crimes. Now he identifies fallen soldiers.

In Odesa, in southern Ukraine, two morgue workers pushed open the heavy, rusted doors of a refrigerated rail carriage that contained the remains of dozens of soldiers killed in battle. A white bag was placed on an autopsy table, and Ruslan Fedorenko, 61, a forensic pathologist, turned to his work.

None of these people carry weapons. But like Ukrainians across the country, they deal with the war and its consequences every day.

Lychakiv Cemetery, the oldest in Lviv, has been a place of sorrow for countless families. For Mr. Biliak, it is a workplace. He is the first to arrive at a gravesite, and one of the last to leave after he and his colleagues shape the mound of earth over it.

This has been his business since 1992, after the Soviet Union collapsed and people clung to whatever work they could find. “We made monuments out of stone chips; back then, a job like that cost $200 to $300, and that was big money,” Mr. Biliak said as he chain-smoked.

At the cemetery’s Field of Honorary Burials, an excavator finished digging out a grave. Mr. Biliak and the other diggers climbed in and began to shape its walls. In a few hours, it would receive the remains of another soldier. The men joked as they worked. Oleksandr Dmytriv, 40, who runs the cemetery, brought them hot coffee.

At 9 a.m., loudspeakers announced the minute of silence that is now observed every day across the country. The joking stopped. Mr. Biliak took his cap off and looked out over hundreds of graves, as the flags of Ukraine and individual military units fluttered over them. He crossed himself three times.

“It’s a disaster,” he said. “You know how it wrecks your head?” He picked up his shovels and walked to a shed, waiting for the funeral to start.

“A horse is a big animal,” said Ms. Buraho, the psychotherapist. “It can step on you or bite you, so a soldier standing next to it can’t stay inside his own memories,” she added. “He has to be here and now.”

She was explaining how horses can help soldiers with post-traumatic stress disorder, as well as problems with balance, joint mobility or vertigo — a process known as hippotherapy.

Each session begins with a circle of trust, where the soldiers talk about themselves and what they expect from the session. Then they are introduced to the horses and practice making contact with the animals.

Ms. Buraho said the exercise teaches soldiers to slow down, observe the horses’ reactions, become more aware of themselves and establish boundaries. A horse can sense aggression and pull away; the soldier has to calm down to restore contact.

Later, they moved into the saddle to focus on body awareness, balance and relaxation as riders swayed and moved with their horses. The horses’ movements send rhythmic pulses through the riders’ bodies that help them reconnect with physical sensations, Ms. Buraho said.

The war has affected her, too. Years of worrying about her family and others have left her exhausted and made it harder to feel joy, she said. She draws strength from nature and from other people, including her 4-year-old grandson, Daniel, who can distinguish the sound of a ballistic missile from that of a Shahed drone. “Don’t be afraid, it’s just a Shahed,” she recalled him telling her.

During the therapy session, some of the soldiers smiled, stroking the horses and leaning into them. At the end, they fed them. “They’re one step closer to healing,” Ms. Buraho said.

Dr. Boiko, who works on the frontline, runs a “stabilization point” where wounded soldiers are rushed for initial treatment. Her facility is in a basement, divided between patients’ rooms and staff living quarters.

Medical staff spend nearly all their time there, because Russian drones make it too dangerous to go outside. “You get used to it,” Dr. Boiko said. “You adapt to everything.”

The facilities are meant for soldiers, but with medical care scarce near the front, civilians are often taken there too. Dr. Boiko remembered treating a woman, at another facility, who had been brought in by a soldier on a motorcycle. One of her legs was gone, lost to a Russian drone. “That stabilization point was later leveled by guided aerial bombs,” Dr. Boiko said.

The medical staff pass free time by watching sports, movies and TV shows. Some relax by smoking hookah. Dr. Boiko said she had no serious relationships, so as not to get attached to anyone. One of her colleagues, a surgeon, has a young daughter whom he sees just once a year, on leave.

“Our motivation is when we find out that a badly wounded man we stabilized made it to the next medical facility, that he’s all right afterward, that we managed to save someone’s limb or life,” Dr. Boiko said.

“I lost everything,” said Dr. Fedorenko, the forensic pathologist.” All I have left is my wife, my son and my car.”

He was remembering Bakhmut, the city in eastern Ukraine that he fled in 2022, now in ruins and under Russian control. “It’s my hometown, and it’s gone,” he said. “It hurts to remember.”

Dr. Fedorenko went into forensic medicine to help solve crimes. Then, in 2014, as the head of Bakhmut’s forensic medicine department, he used his skills to identify fallen soldiers. Russian-backed separatists in the area had begun a low-level insurgency that would persist for years. He worked to identify dozens of war dead in 2015.

But that pales in comparison to what he and his colleagues now handle.

Dr. Fedorenko works on the platform of a railway station. Several autopsy tables stand under a tent covered with camouflage netting. On both sides of the platform are dozens of refrigerated railway carriages containing the bodies of Ukrainian soldiers, each in a white bag marked with a serial number. Some are only burned remains.

Working in protective gear, Dr. Fedorenko takes samples for DNA testing. “We try to identify the fallen as fast as we can, so the body can be sent to the family for burial,” he said.

He gets, at most, two days off a month. He spends as much time as he can with his wife, Nataliia. They walk along the shore of the Black Sea and talk about things that have nothing to do with work.

item.title: Russia and Ukraine Trade Strikes Against Key Bridges
item.description:
The only bridge linking Russia to the occupied Crimean Peninsula was temporarily closed on Tuesday morning after suffering damage from a series of Ukrainian attacks, according to Russian officials.

Overnight, two of the main bridges over the Dnipro River in Kyiv, Ukraine’s capital, were also temporarily closed after Russian strikes on the structures late on Monday, Ukrainian officials said.

The dual strikes on important bridges hundreds of miles from the front lines were part of a long-running battle in Russia’s war against Ukraine, involving logistics, symbols and survival. Bridges are some of the hardest structures to bring down using long-range weapons and such structures have repeatedly defied quick destruction.

The extent of the damage to the Ukrainian and Russian bridges was not immediately clear as engineering teams on both sides were dispatched to assess the aftermath of the attacks.

The Kerch Strait Bridge between Russia and Crimea, a 12-mile span that holds both military and political significance for the Kremlin, suffered structural damage, according to Russia’s Investigative Committee, the country’s equivalent of the F.B.I.

The Russian Transport Ministry said in a statement that road and rail traffic on the bridge had been suspended while inspections were conducted.

“Motorists are advised not to travel toward the Crimean Bridge and to monitor the operational situation in official sources,” the ministry said.

Russia illegally annexed Crimea from Ukraine in 2014, and Kyiv has repeatedly attacked the Kerch Strait Bridge since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. Ukrainian forces have tried, unsuccessfully, to take the bridge down in unconventional sabotage operations and by direct bombardments.

In October 2022, a truck bombing collapsed sections of the bridge and ignited a passing fuel train. Ukrainian forces followed up with a naval drone strike in July 2023 that damaged the road deck. In June 2025, Ukraine carried out an underwater demolition operation in which operatives detonated more than a metric ton of explosives against the bridge’s submerged support pillars.

Kyiv’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko, said on Tuesday that the capital’s Northern and Southern bridges were closed to traffic after the Russian missile attack Monday night.

“We will provide updates as soon as new information becomes available. Municipal services are working on the ground,” Mr. Klitschko said in a statement. “We are doing everything possible to restore traffic as quickly as possible.”

item.title: From Failed Businessman to Accused Plotter in the Killing of Haiti’s Leader
item.description:
He claimed to be a Florida doctor and pastor, but there is no record of him having a U.S. medical degree or leading a church.

He filed for bankruptcy, but his problems really began when he started promoting and broadcasting plans to become Haiti’s president, calling himself the country’s savior and boasting that he had the backing of the U.S. government.

Now, Christian Emmanuel Sanon is on trial in Miami, accused by federal prosecutors of conspiring to kidnap or kill the last elected president of Haiti, Jovenel Moïse, who was assassinated in his bedroom in July 2021.

In court, Mr. Sanon, dressed in a suit and tie, has the bearing of a statesman. But prosecutors say the 67-year-old Haitian American was nothing more than a con man.

The well-spoken Florida resident is accused of teaming up with a South Florida security firm and a hit squad of Colombian former military commandos, who stormed Mr. Moïse’s presidential residence at night and shot him at point-blank range.

The killing plunged Haiti into chaos that continues to grip the country with gangs controlling much of the capital, Port-au-Prince, preventing an election to replace Mr. Moïse. (His widow, Martine Moïse, has registered to run for president in an election that, for now, is scheduled for next year.)

Mr. Sanon was arrested in Haiti a few days after the assassination and jailed. In 2023 he was transferred to U.S. custody, where he was denied bail and remains detained.

Mr. Sanon’s defense team has painted him as a naïve and trusting family man who became a pawn caught in a large multinational plot that he did not believe would end in assassination.

“He doesn’t have a nickel,” Humberto Dominguez, a defense lawyer, told the jury, suggesting that his client lacked the means or political savvy to be the mastermind portrayed by prosecutors.

Mr. Sanon testified in his own defense last week that he loves his country and only wanted to find a way to replace a president he believed was shredding Haiti’s democracy.

Mr. Sanon suggested he was trying to help the United States and even provided information about Islamic extremists suspected of establishing a toehold in Haiti, an issue the F.B.I. had been keenly interested in.

But in his opening statement to the jury, Sean McClaughlin, a prosecutor, described Mr. Sanon as “a repeat failed businessman masquerading as a mega pastor” who was heavily in debt and was driven by greed, arrogance and “a lust for power.”

Mr. Sanon, who was born and raised in Haiti, created a series of companies in Florida under his name, according to state corporate records, but without much success. In 2013, he filed for bankruptcy.

Mr. Sanon, who traveled frequently between Florida and Haiti, had no political experience. But he used his connections in the United States and his fluency in English, French and Creole to pose as an opposition leader who claimed falsely to have influential friends in the U.S. State Department, according to interviews and court records.

Jake Johnston, an expert on Haiti who has followed the Moïse assassination case closely, said Mr. Sanon made those same claims when he spoke with him in 2019.

He learned of Mr. Sanon because he was interested in identifying people trying to influence Haitian politics, said Mr. Johnston, a senior research associate at the Center for Economic and Policy Research in Washington.

During their conversation, Mr. Sanon described “actively making connections” inside the U.S. government who were backing his plan to take over Haiti, Mr. Johnston said. He never took him seriously, Mr. Johnston said, describing Mr. Sanon as “a serial liar with no real connections to power in Haiti.”

Douglas Lofland, a Florida businessman, also recalled Mr. Sanon’s boasting about his connections in the U.S. government in meetings they had in 2019 and 2020.

Introduced by a mutual acquaintance, Mr. Lofland was seeking help to address a dispute over a marble quarry project in Haiti.

“I truly believed he was in contact with people from the U.S. government, but I was beginning to suspect they may have been impostors,” he said. “He would never disclose the names.”

Parnell Duverger, a Haitian American who had taught economics, recalled meeting Mr. Sanon — also through mutual acquaintances — in the fall of 2020 at a pizzeria in South Florida to discuss a wildly ambitious multibillion-dollar development plan for Haiti that Mr. Sanon was floating to attract investors.

The plan envisioned a wide array of projects, including roads, hospitals, airports and seaports. But there was no indication where the financing would come from.

Over six months, Mr. Duverger said he participated in several video meetings that included several people who presented themselves as U.S. government advisers. But, according to evidence federal prosecutors presented in Mr. Sanon’s case, they had nothing to do with the U.S. government.

Mr. Duverger told The New York Times before his death earlier this year that he came to realize that Mr. Sanon’s plans were the result of an oversize ego. “He’s a very audacious, deceptive man,” Mr. Duverger said.

In 2020, Mr. Sanon also held numerous meetings in Haiti with local politicians and civil society leaders, pushing his candidacy, first as a future prime minister, and then as president, according to witness testimony at Mr. Sanon’s trial.

“He was always well dressed, with a tie,” Julio Loiseau, a community activist in Haiti who participated in several of the meetings, said in an interview. “They didn’t call him Pastor Sanon,” he added, referring to others at the meetings. “They called him Mr. President.”

Mr. Loiseau said local politicians would lobby Mr. Sanon for ministerial positions in his future government.

“He said he was sent by the State Department and was on a mission from God,” he added.

Mr. Sanon’s charisma coupled with the long history of U.S. involvement in Haiti, including a military occupation in the early 20th century, made it easier to convince people he had the backing of the United States, according to those who had met Mr. Sanon.

In 2021, Mr. Sanon enlisted a small Miami security firm, Counter Terrorist Unit Federal Academy, in his plans, according to court documents. The firm raised money to pay for weapons, gear and the Colombian mercenaries accused of killing Haiti’s president, prosecutors say. (Four defendants linked to the security firm were found guilty in May by a federal jury in Miami of conspiring in Mr. Moïse’s assassination.)

Mr. Sanon also recorded a video he shared widely that sought to rally people against Mr. Moïse, whom he had accused of human rights violations and plotting to remain in office beyond his term. The video described the president’s residence as a “rat’s nest.”

Mr. Sanon even reached out directly to the State Department in the weeks before the assassination, asking the newly installed Biden administration for help in setting up a transitional government.

“Moïse has stolen the democracy Haitians died to create,” he wrote to a top official, according to a letter entered into evidence in Mr. Sanon’s trial.

The Biden administration never responded to the letter but issued statements supporting Haiti’s official timeline for elections.

Mr. Sanon’s defense asserts that the government’s case has been built with the help of prosecution witnesses who have already pleaded guilty in the assassination plot and are seeking reduced sentences.

The defense also claimed Mr. Sanon had sought to provide information to the F.B.I. about Islamic extremists who were supposedly setting up training camps in Haiti.

F.B.I. agents did meet with Mr. Sanon in April 2021 in Miami but quickly determined he had no useful information, according to testimony from the agents at Mr. Sanon’s trial.

Eventually, the Miami security firm realized that Mr. Sanon never enjoyed the popularity in Haiti he claimed and parted ways with him, witnesses said at the trial.

Still, prosecutors say, Mr. Sanon kept in touch with the assassination plotters right up to the night Mr. Moïse was fatally shot.

“He doesn’t pack up and go away,’’ Mr. McClaughlin told jurors. “He’s still 100 percent a part of the team.’’

When Mr. Sanon learned of Mr. Moïse’s death, the prosecutor said he expressed no shock or surprise, “only satisfaction.”

But in his testimony, Mr. Sanon said he never expressed support for the violent act.

item.title: Tracking China’s War of Words Against Japan
item.description:
When China’s leader, Xi Jinping, met with President Trump at the White House earlier this fall, the two leaders toasted to friendly relations.

But in private, Mr. Xi offered Mr. Trump a stark warning about Japan, a U.S. ally, according to two officials briefed on the talks, who requested anonymity to discuss private conversations. Mr. Xi told Mr. Trump that Japan’s recent military buildup threatened to destabilize Asia, the officials said, and that Mr. Trump should be cautious about working with Japan’s prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, describing her as a “militarist.”

The warning from Mr. Xi was part of a broader effort by China to isolate and undermine Japan after Ms. Takaichi said last year that Japan could be forced to defend Taiwan in case of a Chinese invasion. China considers Taiwan, a self-governed democracy that lies just 69 miles from Japan’s westernmost island, part of its territory.

Since the comments, Mr. Xi has overseen a campaign involving propaganda and diplomacy to target Japan, according to interviews with officials and scholars, and an analysis by The New York Times of Chinese Foreign Ministry briefings and state media. It is all part of a push, analysts say, to persuade the world that Japan is a resurgent aggressor.

The Times found that:

China has deployed words and images to portray Japan as a World War II-era enemy, using phrases like “remilitarization” and “neo-militarism,” and videos that compare Japan to a “rampaging gray rhino.”

Chinese officials have repeatedly sought to belittle Ms. Takaichi, Japan’s first female prime minister, omitting her title in official briefings, breaking with longstanding practice. State media has depicted Ms. Takaichi in short skirts and a nurse’s uniform in cartoons, and described her as “Abe’s girl,” referring to Shinzo Abe, the former Japanese prime minister and Ms. Takaichi’s mentor.

In private conversations with Western scholars, Chinese academics have recently pushed the narrative that Japan is the “Israel of East Asia,” poised to lead the United States into conflict and destabilize the region.

Russia has helped amplify China’s talking points, branding Japan as a threat. Moscow has echoed Beijing in describing Japan as an “enemy state” that is not to be trusted, invoking a World War II-era designation used against former Axis powers.

Mr. Xi and Ms. Takaichi will cross paths this week at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit meeting in Shenzhen, China. The encounter is expected to be frosty; Mr. Xi might try to use the summit as an opportunity to alienate Ms. Takaichi from Japan’s allies, experts say.

The analysis covered Chinese state-run and Communist Party-run outlets, including China Central Television, the Xinhua news agency, Global Times and People’s Liberation Army Daily.

China has long been at odds with Japan. But the current scale and coordination of its campaign have little modern precedent, experts said.

“Anti-Japan propaganda is just absolutely everywhere now,” said David Bandurski, executive director of the China Media Project, an independent research group. “It’s a far more focused use of anti-Japanese framing than we’ve seen at any point.”

Ms. Takaichi told Japan’s Parliament on Nov. 7, 2025, that any attempt by China to blockade or seize Taiwan could constitute a “survival-threatening situation” for Japan, implying a potential military response. Her comments reflected a long-held Japanese view, but one that has rarely been verbalized.

China reacted furiously. The government urged millions of tourists to avoid Japan, limited the export of some critical minerals, restricted Japanese seafood imports and increased patrols in disputed waters.

Mr. Xi appears to be concerned that Ms. Takaichi, a close American ally who has been a critic of China, could get in the way of China’s military and economic expansion in Asia. Analysts said that he is seeking to drive a wedge between Japan and the United States, as well as countries like Australia, South Korea, India and the United Kingdom.

Ms. Takaichi has accelerated a military buildup to counter China, raising military spending to 2 percent of gross domestic product two years ahead of schedule and loosening postwar rules that restricted the export of weapons. She is expected to push for even more military spending next month as part of a new national security strategy.

In the year since Ms. Takaichi’s comments on Taiwan, China has sharply escalated its rhetorical attacks on Japan, according to the Times’s analysis, and there has been a surge in propaganda aimed at both domestic and global audiences.

Since last November, the Chinese Foreign Ministry has publicly accused Tokyo of “remilitarization” or “neo-militarism” at more than 60 briefings, the analysis found. People’s Daily, the Communist Party mouthpiece, cited Japanese “neo-militarism” in 65 articles, and warnings of Japanese “militarism” surged across the outlets we analyzed.

Chinese officials have repeatedly invoked the image of a “gray rhino,” a phrase used in Chinese to describe a looming threat, to characterize Japan. One video that circulated on Chinese news sites, generated by artificial intelligence, shows a rhino, draped in a rising sun flag, wreaking havoc across land and sea.

China Daily, a state-controlled news organization aimed at an international audience, published a cartoon in May showing Ms. Takaichi dressed in samurai armor and carrying a sword. A People’s Daily cartoon describes Japan’s military ambitions as “sugarcoated poison,” showing Ms. Takaichi wrapping skulls to give to children.

The Times parsed more than 20,000 transcripts from the Chinese Foreign Ministry’s briefings since 2013; nearly 400,000 articles in People’s Daily; more than 100,000 items from Guangming Daily, P.L.A. Daily, Global Times and Xinhua; and thousands of published readouts of Chinese leaders’ meetings, state broadcasts, ministry releases and social media trends.

The analysis found that Chinese media has helped amplify official messaging. When interest in China’s feud with Japan faded from April to June and questions from foreign news outlets fell, reporters from state-controlled media in China tried to keep the story alive by asking about Japan at a far higher rate than before.

In December, a TV reporter from Shenzhen noted that scholars across the region were warning of Japan’s “remilitarization,” prompting a spokesman for the Chinese Foreign Ministry to answer with a list of Japan’s wartime atrocities. In August, on the anniversary of the bombing of Hiroshima, a Xinhua reporter said at a news briefing that “81 years later, Japan’s right-wing forces are stirring, plotting to restore militarism.”

The propaganda has sometimes spilled into the policy arena. When China’s Commerce Ministry placed 80 Japanese industrial, defense and research listings on export control blacklists and watch lists this year, a stated goal was to curb “remilitarization” and “neo-militarism.”

Mr. Xi’s government has made a point of singling out Ms. Takaichi. A year after taking office, she is still relatively popular at home and has been a vocal supporter of Taiwan throughout her career. She has also built a warm relationship with Mr. Trump.

One tactic used by the Chinese government is to omit Ms. Takaichi’s title, a pointed break with diplomatic protocol. From July through September, officials dropped “prime minister” in six of seven mentions of Ms. Takaichi.

On Weibo, a popular Chinese social media site that is heavily curated by the government, hashtags that mocked Ms. Takaichi’s wardrobe, emotions, voice or hugging style trended at least 30 times over the past year, the analysis found.

China also appears to be working to foment opposition to Ms. Takaichi inside Japan’s political system. Chinese officials have tried to persuade visiting delegations of Japanese lawmakers and executives recently that Ms. Takaichi does not understand the economic risks of her tough approach to China, and that they should stand up to her, according to two people briefed on the conversations.

After one such meeting in September, Wang Yi, China’s foreign minister, said that it was time for Japan to “correct the erroneous words and deeds” of its leader.

In trying to stir concern about Japan, Chinese scholars have told their counterparts in the West that Ms. Takaichi’s Japan is becoming the “Israel of East Asia.” A delegation of Chinese scholars in South Korea used the phrase during a recent meeting with American scholars, according to David Sacks, an expert on China at the Council on Foreign Relations who took part in the meeting.

Mr. Sacks said his Chinese counterparts repeatedly raised concerns about Japanese militarism. They told the Americans that they feared Japan was seeking to become the most powerful country in East Asia and could draw the United States into conflict.

The aim, Mr. Sacks said, was to push Mr. Trump to “rein in Japan.”

“They want the United States to tell its ally to knock it off and to de-escalate with Beijing,” he said.

During his visit to the White House earlier this year, Mr. Xi suggested that Mr. Trump should join China’s efforts to counter Japan. Mr. Xi invoked World War II to highlight friendship between Beijing and Washington and cited Japan as a common enemy. He described Imperial Japan as “fascist” and “militarist” aggressors.

China and Russia have increasingly reinforced each other’s attacks on Japan, the analysis shows, using common terms like “remilitarization.”

Analysts say it is all part of President Vladimir V. Putin’s recent pressure campaign against Japan. In August, he made his first-ever visit to islands claimed by both Moscow and Tokyo. Last month, Russia detained a Japanese journalist on espionage charges. And in recent days, Mr. Putin has seized Russian assets of Japan Tobacco.

During a visit to Beijing in May, Mr. Putin signed a statement with Mr. Xi that included a lengthy section devoted to denouncing Japan’s military moves. The statement said, “Japan’s current acceleration of ‘remilitarization’ poses a serious threat to regional peace and stability.” The statement added that Japan should “resist ‘new militarism’ and ‘remilitarization.’”

During an appearance in Moscow last month, Mr. Putin said that he wanted good relations with Japan. But he added, “We are concerned by Japan’s plans for militarization.”

Methodology

The Times collected hundreds of thousands of documents from multiple official Chinese sources: China’s Foreign Ministry briefings, articles from People’s Daily, P.L.A. Daily, Guangming Daily, Global Times, China Daily and Xinhua, as well as Chinese military, ministry, broadcast and social media records. Most sources were downloaded from official websites, and the rest from public digital archives, like the Internet Archive. To quantify the appearance of terms like “remilitarization,” “rearmament” and “neo-militarism” in Foreign Ministry briefings, we used A.I. models developed by Anthropic and Google, Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Carbon, to strip out reporters’ questions and measure phrase frequencies per 1,000 Chinese characters. We also used A.I. to separate official statements from third-party quotes, generate initial translations, and classify the topic of news stories, briefing questions and social media trends.

Every quote and translation used in the story was verified against the original Chinese records.

Murphy Zhao contributed reporting from Hong Kong, and Kiuko Notoya from Tokyo.

item.title: First Her Daughter. Now Her Grandson. A Family’s Hospital Nightmare.
item.description:
Gorette Mbusi stood on her doorstep and wrestled with a question. Should she let her grandson be taken to the hospital?

Health workers had come to her village, in the eastern part of the Democratic Republic of Congo, to implore her to let them take the young man to a specialized Ebola facility in the nearby town of Nizi. But she was wary. She had already lost two family members, including her daughter, who had been transported to the hospital and then died.

Now, her grandson was sick.

“I don’t know where this sickness is coming from that is killing my family,” she said. “I feel abandoned.”

Ms. Mbusi’s dilemma reflects a central challenge for health workers as they struggle to contain the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak on record — how to stop people from passing the disease to loved ones at home.

Community transmission happens when family members care for Ebola patients at home and then become ill themselves, spreading the disease and making it more difficult for medical teams to identify and isolate people who have been in contact with those infected. Tracking and tracing the contacts of Ebola patients and educating people about the virus are crucial to ending community transmission.

Health workers must first get more people to seek medical treatment in hospitals sooner and overcome deep suspicions about Ebola in villages like this one, known as Nizi 4.

There are those who doubt Ebola is real or say it’s a curse. Others think they will be imprisoned if they enter a hospital. Medical facilities also carry their own risks. If a hospital does not have ample testing or strict safety protocols, a patient with an illness that might be mistaken for Ebola, such as malaria, could end up being exposed to Ebola itself, a far more fatal disease.

For many Congolese, home and family are sanctuaries in a region tormented by decades of insurgent violence and broken government institutions.

While Ms. Mbusi’s grandson, Dieumerci Koli, 17, languished on a mattress, she held her ground. Throughout her ordeal, she referred to her grandchildren as her children. Fearing another loss, she refused to take Dieumerci to the hospital.

The deadlock was broken only when the village’s acting chief, Dieudonne Musingu, entered the home and appealed to her to listen to the Congolese health workers.

When she relented, the young man stumbled into the light, blood dripping from his mouth and nose. I watched, along with some neighbors, as he staggered to a waiting ambulance. We kept our distance. Halfway up the hill, he sat down on a patch of bare earth and looked up at the nearby trees. It was close to his house but he appeared disoriented.

Because Congo’s Ebola response struggles with limited resources, the ambulance sent to transport Dieumerci was an aging four-wheel drive staffed by a Congolese man who wore little protective gear.

“Of course I’m afraid,” said the ambulance driver, wearing only a mask and one glove to protect himself from infection.

Ms. Mbusi, 62, climbed aboard with her grandson and his 5-year-old brother, Fabrice Koli. The young man spent the ride clinging to his grandmother, she said.

When the family arrived at the Ebola clinic, the staff said there were no beds available in the isolation unit. Ms. Mbusi and her two grandsons were forced to wait in the hot sun for an hour.

Dieumerci was eventually given a bed in an isolation room, where nurses gave him an IV. He was barely conscious, but within 30 minutes he sat up and could say his name.

Dr. Patient Wenga, the clinic’s lead doctor, said the young man had a chance to recover, even though he had been brought to the hospital so late.

But Dieumerci died that night.

As of November, more than 5,300 people have died in this Ebola outbreak. More than 11,000 people have been infected, according to the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Even when families seek help in hospitals, they do not always survive. The death rate for Bundibugyo, the virus responsible for this Ebola outbreak, is nearly 50 percent. Scientists have yet to find a cure, and by the time many patients see a doctor in a hospital, they are often near death.

The Africa C.D.C. reported on Thursday that 64 percent of Ebola deaths in the last week of October took place outside a hospital.

Dr. Wenga said critically ill Ebola patients that arrived to his hospital often died overnight, when staffing was thin. Dieumerci died just before dawn, the doctor said.

That morning, Ms. Mbusi wept as health workers zipped her grandson into a body bag. Friends later said he was a quiet young man who, like most people in the village, worked at a small-scale gold mine on a nearby hillside.

“We worked together, drank beer together, smoked together and went to church together,” said David Dhalonga Boju, a fellow miner.

Two days later, Dieumerci was buried by Congolese health workers, who carried his body in a simple coffin down the hillside and placed it in a fresh grave next to his aunt and sister, who also died from the disease. His friends sang mourning songs in Swahili.

Ms. Mbusi was not able to attend the funeral. She and Fabrice had come down with headaches and fever, early signs of the virus. Fabrice later tested positive.

Amid the heartbreak, health workers said that they had made progress in the village. When the outreach team first arrived in September, residents shut their doors. Several villagers had shown Ebola symptoms, but refused to accept outside medical help, said Mr. Musingu, the acting chief.

Half of those who died of Ebola in Nizi in September died at home, according to the Africa C.D.C.

Yet, since then, a shift has happened. The day after Dieumerci’s funeral, Congolese workers held a public meeting on the main street of the village. The mayor and church leaders came to speak, along with a local woman named Micheline Mbidha, 41.

Ms. Mbidha had been treated for Ebola at the hospital in Nizi. She said that when she first showed symptoms in July, she immediately sent her six children out of the home and took herself to the hospital. None of her children were infected with Ebola, she said at the meeting.

She added that she had warned her neighbor, Ms. Mbusi, not to treat family members at home. “People in the village have a serious problem accepting that Ebola is real,” Ms. Mbidha said.

After the meeting, Dr. Leon Malengala, who leads the World Health Organization’s outreach team in Nizi, said villagers had started reporting to health workers when they felt sick.

“At the beginning, there was strong resistance to our operation in the village, but now that’s starting to change,” he said.

At the Ebola clinic, Ms. Mbusi endured another harrowing week. A close female relative was brought in and placed in a room two doors down from where she and Fabrice were isolated. The relative died two days later.

Ms. Mbusi’s health, however, remained stable, and she did not require intensive care. Fabrice was given an IV for rehydration and was closely monitored by medical staff.

Each day in isolation, Ms. Mbusi and her grandson would sit in the sun on plastic chairs outside their room and talk to other patients who were isolated in the ward with Ebola symptoms.

After a week in the hospital, Dr. Wenga said that both Ms. Mbusi and Fabrice had received negative Ebola tests. A second test would be performed soon, he said. If that, too, was negative, he would be able to give his patients some good news: They could go home.
